chapters.title: Official Lecturer Samples — Original Questions
chapters.description: Ten official samples, wording and options retained. Answers and explanations are AI-inferred, not an official marking key. Keep answer shuffling OFF because some choices refer to option letters.

questions.stem: Which of the following is / are considered to be consequentialist ethical theories:

options.text: Utilitarianism
Egoism
Deontology
a) and b) above
a), b) and c) above

questions.explanation: AI-inferred answer; no official answer key was supplied. Utilitarianism and egoism are consequentialist theories; deontology is not. The complete answer is a) and b).
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample 1 — https://ucc.instructure.com/courses/93031/files/11010257?module_item_id=3181356; answer support: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 1 — Introduction to Ethical Theories and Frameworks; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 2 — Utilitarianism; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 3 — Egoism

questions.stem: In the ‘Capital Punishment Experiment’ (Lord et al., 1979 ), discussed in class, both supporters and opponents of capital punishment were presented with the same samples of research that showed that capital punishment can be an effective deterrent and also the same samples of research that showed that capital punishment is not an effective deterrent. Which ONE of the following is TRUE:

options.text: By exposing both camps (those for and against capital punishment) to research that presented an opposing view to their own, it served to make both camps even more polarised in their positions regarding their perceived effectiveness of capital punishment.

By exposing both camps (those for and against capital punishment) to research that presented an opposing view to their own, it served to make both camps narrow their positions (i.e. come closer) regarding their perceived effectiveness of capital punishment.

By exposing both camps (those for and against capital punishment) to research that presented an opposing view to their own, it made no difference to their perceived effectiveness of capital punishment that they held prior to reviewing any research, and both camps remained the same distance apart.
Those who support capital punishment only read the research that confirmed the effectiveness of the deterrent effect of capital punishment.
Those who oppose capital punishment only read the research that confirms that capital punishment has no deterrent effect

questions.explanation: AI-inferred answer; no official answer key was supplied. The same mixed evidence increased polarisation as each group gave more weight to belief-consistent findings.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample 2 — https://ucc.instructure.com/courses/93031/files/11010257?module_item_id=3181356; answer support: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: Which of the following is true?

options.text: The Milgram Shock Experiment was undertaken to explore the degree to which regular people would inflict pain on other regular people if instructed to do so by an authority figure.
The Stanford Prison Experiment was undertaken to explore the degree to which regular people would inflict pain on other regular people if instructed to do so by an authority figure.

The Milgram Shock Experiment transpired to be more effective than the Stanford Prison Experiment in showing that regular people would inflict pain on other regular people when instructed to do so by an authority figure, as there were more controls in the former on how much pain could be inflicted on the learners at each point, whereas in the latter experiment the research participants were just instructed to inflict pain on the prisoners as they saw fit.
a and b above
a, b and c above

questions.explanation: AI-inferred answer; no official answer key was supplied. Milgram directly tested obedience to an authority asking participants to administer shocks. The Stanford study’s stated purpose concerned roles, norms and expectations in a simulated prison; it is not the same controlled shock-obedience design, and c) is not supported.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample 3 — https://ucc.instructure.com/courses/93031/files/11010257?module_item_id=3181356; answer support: Reading 2 — The Milgram Shock Experiment; Stanford experiment purpose checked against https://www.prisonexp.org/faq

questions.stem: In terms of Stakeholder Theory, which of the following is NOT considered to be a type of stakeholder:

options.text: Diffused
Normative
Enabling
Participative
Functional

questions.explanation: AI-inferred answer; no official answer key was supplied. The assigned classification includes diffused, normative, enabling and functional stakeholders. Participative is not one of those named categories.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample 4 — https://ucc.instructure.com/courses/93031/files/11010257?module_item_id=3181356; answer support: Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82)

questions.stem: Brian is a student, and he works part-time in the deli-counter of a busy city-centre shop. Any left-over food is always given to the residents of a near-by hostel for the homeless. On this particular Saturday evening, Brian is given a parcel of left-over sandwiches and asked to drop them off at the shelter on his way home. Brian is feeling peckish after a long shift, and is heading out for the night with his friends. He also knows that the food is intended for the residents of the homeless shelter, and it's 'not right' that he should take it for his himself. He could have bought food for himself from the deli at a staff discount. However, he also reasons that he already does more for the homeless than most other people, and certainly any of his friends, as he volunteers for a 'soup run' for the homeless every Thursday night (and has being doing this regularly for over two years now). Having considered this, he doesn't think it's so bad that he should now take the sandwiches back to his house, and he walks straight past the shelter for the homeless. This is an example of which ONE of the following:

options.text: Self-serving Bias
Instant-entitlement Bias
‘Bathsheba Syndrome’
Moral licence
Personal Positivity Bias

questions.explanation: AI-inferred answer; no official answer key was supplied. Brian treats earlier good conduct as moral credit licensing a later wrongful act, rather than performing a good act to compensate afterwards.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample 5 — https://ucc.instructure.com/courses/93031/files/11010257?module_item_id=3181356; answer support: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: With reference to the case-study, ‘ Casas Bahia – Marketing to the Poor’, which one of the following is FALSE:

options.text: Casas Bahia, at the time of the case-study, was making around 90% of its revenues from credit sales.
Casa Bahia advertised that they offered lower credit rates than most other retailers, which was true.

Many customers were not financially literate (or interested) enough to distinguish between the cost of the products they bought with or without credit, as they were more concerned with the overall price they were paying and whether they could afford this or not. Casas Bahia has been criticised for possibly playing on this uncertainty.

As a sign of good-will, on one occasion in 2002, Samuel Klein offered all clients in arrears, nearly one million of them, a full pardon on their debt. There was no immediate financial benefit to the company, but it was an effective marketing tool, as it brought back some customers who had defaulted previously.
Casas Bahia had a relatively low default rate on its credit sales generally, though it varied somewhat by product type.

questions.explanation: AI-inferred answer; no official answer key was supplied. The original case describes the debt write-off as providing a tax deduction as well as a marketing benefit, and concerns debts defaulted before 1997. The statement that there was no immediate financial benefit is therefore false.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample 6 — https://ucc.instructure.com/courses/93031/files/11010257?module_item_id=3181356; answer support: Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor

questions.stem: According to Pretty et al. (2016), in the article ‘ Improving Health and Well-being Independently of GDP’ (a core reading for the module and also discussed in a lecture), the authors present a list of the increasing negative externalities (costs) associated with six key variables that should contribute to well-being (such as ‘healthy food’, ‘active mind’ etc.) and a ‘counterbalance’ of positive outcomes related to each of these variables. For instance, an indicator of a negative externality for ‘healthy food’ is increasing obesity levels in adults and children and a countertrend for ‘healthy food’ would be a greater understanding of food sources and sustainability of agriculture. At the end of the study they conclude that “on balance” their ‘scorecard’ for the six factors overall is:

options.text: Very clear, with each factor showing greater improvements overall (in terms of the countertrends) versus the costs of the negative externalities.
Very clear, with each factor showing greater losses (in terms of the negative externalities) overall than the benefits of the improvements (countertrends).
Mixed, but with most factors in substantial deficit (in terms of negative externalities versus positive countertrends).
Mixed, but with most factors in a slight surplus (in terms of positive countertrends versus negative externalities)
Mixed, with half the factors in surplus and the other half in deficit in terms of the balance of negative externalities and positive countertrends.

questions.explanation: AI-inferred answer; no official answer key was supplied. Pretty et al. describe a mixed scorecard with most factors in substantial deficit, rather than a uniformly positive or evenly balanced result.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample 7 — https://ucc.instructure.com/courses/93031/files/11010257?module_item_id=3181356; answer support: Reading 10 — Improving wellbeing independently of GDP

questions.stem: ‘ Enlightened Self-interest’ means that companies act in a way that is considered ‘enlightened’ (beneficial to others / to society) but that is also of commercial benefit to the company itself because:

options.text: It can enhance long-term revenue, such as by keeping loyal customers and / or good employees.
It can help maintain a social licence that makes it easier to operate, such as having the support of the local community
It can help to manage risk and uncertainty, such as by influencing legislation in a pro- active way
A and B above
A, B and C above

questions.explanation: AI-inferred answer; no official answer key was supplied. All three listed benefits can contribute to longer-term commercial self-interest: retention, social licence and management of risk or uncertainty.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample 8 — https://ucc.instructure.com/courses/93031/files/11010257?module_item_id=3181356; answer support: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 3 — Egoism; Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: According to the prescribed (core) reading from the textbook for this module (‘ Business Ethics’ OpenStax, 2018), with regard to the section on Utilitarianism, J S Mill’s ‘ harm principle ’ states that:

options.text: Any harm done by an action must be counter-weighed by any benefit that action has brought, and only then it can be determined if that action is ‘unethical’ or not.

You must never do any harm intentionally to anyone, under any circumstances, regardless of the outcome overall of that action for the population as a whole (as an exception to the overall philosophy of ‘utilitarianism’).
The only reason for power to be rightfully exercised over any individual against their will is to prevent harm to others, and not to the individual themselves.
Power can and should be rightfully exercised over individuals against their will if it will prevent harm to others and / or to the individual themselves.
The potential to cause harm is never reasonable grounds for power to be exercised over any individual against their will, as it can never be proven that any harm would definitely occur.

questions.explanation: AI-inferred answer; no official answer key was supplied. Mill’s harm principle distinguishes preventing harm to others from coercion merely for the individual’s own good.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample 9 — https://ucc.instructure.com/courses/93031/files/11010257?module_item_id=3181356; answer support: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 2 — Utilitarianism; Reading 5 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 44–53)

questions.stem: According to Rawl’s ‘ difference principle’ , discussed in class:

options.text: No one in society should ever be treated differently when considering how the economy is structured, and hierarchies in companies and organisations should be as flat as possible.
Inequality in society is unacceptable and all economic systems should ensure everyone is given an equal share of the rewards of production.
Economic inequality in society is acceptable once the advantages that result from this inequality (such as a new productivity policy) benefit the most disadvantaged groups proportionately.
Ethical values can be interpreted differently when considering cultural factors, but any difference must be clearly indicated by management.
A difference of opinion is not a valid basis for adhering to accepted ethical frameworks

questions.explanation: AI-inferred answer; no official answer key was supplied. Among the supplied options, c) matches the module’s account of the difference principle. Rawls’s concern is with the position of the least advantaged, not merely an increase in total wealth; the original compressed wording is retained.
questions.source: Official MG2008 lecturer sample 10 — https://ucc.instructure.com/courses/93031/files/11010257?module_item_id=3181356; answer support: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences; Reading 6 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 54–58)

chapters.title: Week 1 — Introduction
chapters.description: Reading allocation follows the module outline; lecture questions retain delivered-week placement. Five options; single answer; AI-written practice.

questions.stem: With reference to the definition of business ethics introduced in this module, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.text: The study of business situations, activities and decisions involving questions of right and wrong.
The study of personal beliefs, excluding the responsibilities attached to professional roles.
The study of whether business decisions comply with the criminal law, rather than wider values.
The study of how managers can maximise profit while treating moral judgements as private matters.
The study of charitable spending as a separate activity from ordinary business decisions.

questions.explanation: Business ethics concerns judgements about right and wrong in business decisions; it is broader than accounting, criminal compliance or philanthropy alone.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 1 — Introduction to Business Ethics

questions.stem: A clothing retailer obtains legal advice confirming that its purchasing arrangements comply with the applicable legislation. Its managers are nevertheless told that the arrangements may cause avoidable harm to workers. They reply that, because no law has been broken, there is no further issue to consider. Which ONE of the following best evaluates their position?

options.text: Legal compliance does not remove the need to examine the ethical concerns.
Ethical analysis should be deferred until a specific new legal rule is introduced.
Worker welfare is relevant to ethics only where the retailer directly employs the workers.
Legal compliance settles the ethical issue unless a court first finds a breach.
The existence of an ethical concern establishes that the retailer has broken the law.

questions.explanation: Law establishes enforceable requirements, but lawful conduct can still create ethical conflicts or avoidable harm.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 1 — Introduction to Business Ethics

questions.stem: According to Friedman’s argument about the social responsibility of business, which ONE of the following descriptions of the pursuit of profit is correct?

options.text: Pursuing profits even through deception, provided shareholders receive a return.
Replacing shareholders’ commercial objectives with executives’ private moral preferences.
Giving executives unrestricted authority to spend company funds on their preferred causes.
Giving all stakeholders an identical claim on the company’s profits.
Pursuing profits within open competition and without deception or fraud.

questions.explanation: Friedman’s profit argument is qualified by open competition without deception or fraud; it does not authorise dishonest profit-making.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 1 — Introduction to Business Ethics

questions.stem: An executive proposes using company resources to support a social campaign that the executive personally favours. Some shareholders support the campaign and others do not. With reference to Friedman’s shareholder-agency argument, which ONE of the following most accurately identifies the objection to the executive treating this as an entirely personal choice?

options.text: The executive can have no personal moral commitments outside the business.
Any social expenditure necessarily reduces every shareholder’s long-term return.
A social initiative can never have a legitimate commercial purpose.
The executive is acting as an agent of the owners, rather than spending only their own money.
Shareholders are unable to donate their own money to a social cause.

questions.explanation: The agency objection concerns executives committing resources belonging to the owners, rather than choosing how to spend only their personal money.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 1 — Introduction to Business Ethics

questions.stem: A defence barrister learns information that makes the barrister personally believe a client is guilty. The barrister considers disclosing it because this would satisfy a personal commitment to justice, although disclosure would breach the obligations of the professional relationship. This illustrates which ONE of the following distinctions?

options.text: Professional codes eliminate the possibility of difficult moral judgements.
A morally motivated action cannot breach a professional obligation.
Personal morality can conflict with the ethical obligations of a professional role.
Confidentiality is relevant only when the barrister agrees with the client’s conduct.
Professional ethics simply requires acting on the strongest personal conviction.

questions.explanation: Personal commitments and the obligations of a professional relationship can pull in different directions; a desire for justice does not by itself settle professional conduct.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 1 — Introduction to Business Ethics; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: With reference to the reasons given for studying business ethics, which option gives the COMPLETE set of correct statements below?

options.text: Corporate power and influence can create ethical responsibilities.
Stakeholder demands and employee pressures can raise ethical conflicts.
Existing law already resolves every conflict of values in business.
a) and b) above.
a), b) and c) above.

questions.explanation: Corporate influence and pressures from stakeholders and employees are reasons to study ethics. The claim that law already resolves every value conflict is not.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 1 — Introduction to Business Ethics

chapters.title: Week 2 — Ethics v Morals
chapters.description: Reading allocation follows the module outline; lecture questions retain delivered-week placement. Five options; single answer; AI-written practice.

questions.stem: Aoife has recently joined a sales team. She is uncomfortable with a practice that customers would find misleading, but established colleagues tell her that this is simply how the team works. Without receiving a direct instruction from management, she begins to do the same thing so that she will fit in. This is most directly an example of which ONE of the following?

options.text: Moral compensation.
False consensus.
Fundamental attribution error.
Self-serving bias.
Conformity bias.

questions.explanation: Conformity means taking cues from a group and adapting conduct to fit its norms, even where an employee privately has doubts.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: After a successful project, a manager says that the result demonstrates the manager’s exceptional ability. When a similar project fails, the manager says that the team’s poor performance was responsible. Which ONE of the following best describes this pattern?

options.text: Loss aversion.
Conformity bias.
Self-serving bias.
Biased assimilation.
Moral licensing.

questions.explanation: Self-serving bias attributes success to oneself while shifting responsibility for failure to others or circumstances.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: An employee would normally refuse to approve a questionable transaction. On learning that an existing job may be lost unless a target is met, however, the employee becomes willing to take a risk that would not have been taken merely to obtain an equivalent new opportunity. This most directly illustrates which ONE of the following?

options.text: False consensus.
Moral compensation.
Loss aversion.
Personal positivity bias.
Conformity bias.

questions.explanation: Loss aversion can encourage unusually risky action to avoid an existing loss compared with an equivalent prospective gain.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: In the capital-punishment research discussed in the module, people holding opposing views evaluated research that included evidence on both sides. With reference to biased assimilation, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.text: People displaying biased assimilation refuse to read any evidence that challenges their position.
Equal access to evidence ensures that groups assign equal weight to its conclusions.
Presenting evidence against a belief necessarily causes people to abandon that belief.
People can evaluate the same mixed evidence differently, favouring evidence consistent with their existing beliefs.
Polarisation occurs only when each side is given a different set of research findings.

questions.explanation: Biased assimilation concerns how people assess evidence. Equal access to mixed evidence need not result in equal weighting or convergence.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: A buyer has volunteered regularly for a community organisation for several years. When asked to justify a dishonest claim for expenses, the buyer says that someone who has already done so much good should be allowed this small exception. The buyer is not trying to repair an earlier dishonest act through volunteering. This is an example of which ONE of the following?

options.text: Fundamental attribution error.
Moral compensation.
False consensus.
Moral licensing.
Loss aversion.

questions.explanation: Moral licensing uses previous good conduct as moral credit to justify later questionable conduct.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: After deliberately misleading a customer, a salesperson feels uncomfortable about the kind of person they have become. The following day the salesperson donates to charity in an effort to restore a sense of being a good person. This is most directly an example of which ONE of the following?

options.text: Moral licensing.
False consensus.
Instant-entitlement bias.
Conformity bias.
Moral compensation.

questions.explanation: Moral compensation attempts to restore moral credit after a bad act; it is the reverse sequence from licensing.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: A supervisor describes an employee who falsified a report as simply a bad person. In doing so, the supervisor gives little attention to threats of dismissal, unrealistic targets or pressure from the employee’s team. Which ONE of the following errors is most directly illustrated?

options.text: Moral licensing.
Fundamental attribution error.
Self-serving bias.
Loss aversion.
False consensus.

questions.explanation: Fundamental attribution error overweights character while underweighting situational influences on another person’s behaviour.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: A company founder is confident that the public shares the founder’s views about acceptable advertising. No evidence about public opinion has been collected; the founder simply assumes that these personal views are much more widely held than they actually are. Which ONE of the following best describes this?

options.text: Moral compensation.
Bathsheba syndrome.
Fundamental attribution error.
False consensus.
Conformity bias.

questions.explanation: False consensus overestimates how widely others share one’s own beliefs and attitudes.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: A successful executive begins to argue that ordinary rules are intended for less capable people. The executive deliberately ignores those rules, believing that personal influence will make it possible to control any consequences. Which ONE of the following concepts is the closest fit?

options.text: Conformity bias.
Biased assimilation.
Bathsheba syndrome.
Moral compensation.
Fundamental attribution error.

questions.explanation: The Bathsheba example concerns powerful people regarding ordinary rules as applying to others while expecting to control the consequences themselves.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: A company replaces the word “bribe” in its internal communications with the term “facilitation payment”. With reference to the lecture’s discussion of language and organisational conduct, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.text: Calling a bribe a “facilitation payment” can distance people from the ethical meaning of the action.
Using an accepted industry term establishes that a payment is ethically justified.
Changing the description of a payment is sufficient to change its legal status.
Euphemistic language matters only when employees have never recognised the underlying issue.
A technical description makes the recipient’s consent ethically irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Euphemistic language can obscure the ethical significance of an action; a new label does not by itself alter its legal or moral character.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: With reference to the distinction between ethics and morality in the Week 2 material, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.text: Morality concerns norms, values and beliefs about right and wrong; ethics includes the reasoned study and examination of those moral standards.
Ethics consists only of describing what is common, without examining what ought to be done.
A moral conviction establishes that every action taken in its name satisfies the relevant professional obligations.
Morality means only a company’s written code, whereas ethics means only the private preferences of its directors.
Ethics and morality are defined in the module as unrelated matters that cannot conflict with a professional role.

questions.explanation: The deck distinguishes embedded moral norms from the reasoned examination of morality, while recognising that the terms are sometimes used interchangeably.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: A manager makes an immediate decision that favours a preferred candidate. Only afterwards does the manager construct an elaborate account of why the decision was fair, without reconsidering the original choice. With reference to the behavioural material, this is most directly an example of which ONE of the following?

options.text: False consensus.
Moral rationalisation.
Moral compensation.
Fundamental attribution error.
Loss aversion.

questions.explanation: Moral rationalisation can supply reasons after an intuitive or impulsive decision rather than describe an independent process that produced it.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: A person is assigned to lead a group distributing shared goods. Although the leadership role creates no agreed entitlement to a larger allocation, the person immediately takes more than the others. According to the leadership discussion in the module, this most directly illustrates which ONE of the following?

options.text: Instant-entitlement bias.
False consensus.
Moral compensation.
Biased assimilation.
Fundamental attribution error.

questions.explanation: The entitlement example concerns people taking a larger share after being assigned a leadership position, rather than earning an agreed additional entitlement.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: With reference to bureaucracy and unethical conduct in organisations, which ONE of the following statements is FALSE?

options.text: Allocating work across many roles removes each person’s need to consider the foreseeable effects of their contribution.
Organisational distance can affect how responsibility is perceived.
Examining the organisation does not require ignoring the decisions of individuals within it.
Routine procedures may make harmful practices appear normal.
Dividing work across roles can make it harder for an individual to see the full consequences.

questions.explanation: Division of labour can obscure consequences, but it does not establish that all personal ethical responsibility disappears.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: A director continues to interpret every ambiguous report about a favoured leader positively because that leader was the director’s original choice. The director finds it difficult to recognise contrary evidence about the person they supported. Which ONE of the following concepts from the leadership material is the closest fit?

options.text: Instant-entitlement bias.
Loss aversion.
Fundamental attribution error.
Personal positivity bias.
Moral compensation.

questions.explanation: The deck describes the tendency to see the good in people one elects or supports, connecting it with confirmation bias and cognitive dissonance.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 2 — Ethical Behaviour: Stanford Prison and Milgram

questions.stem: According to the Penneys reading on ethics and price, which ONE of the following best describes the apparent paradox in consumer behaviour?

options.text: A supplier code establishes that all factory conditions meet the stated standard.
Expressing concern guarantees a sustained change in purchasing behaviour.
Consumers can express concern about production ethics while continuing to buy mainly on price.
Low prices demonstrate that consumers have no ethical concerns.
A purchase reveals every factor the consumer considered and the weight attached to each.

questions.explanation: The Penneys reading highlights a gap between stated ethical concern and price-driven purchasing; expressed attitudes do not guarantee sustained behavioural change.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 1 — Penneys: ethics–price paradox

questions.stem: According to the Penneys reading, consumers may know about poor working conditions but expect other people to take action. Which ONE of the following best describes the process involved?

options.text: The disappearance of an ethical concern once several people recognise it.
The acceptance of responsibility through purchasing at the lowest available price.
The transfer of all ethical responsibility to consumers rather than retailers.
The diffusion of responsibility among people who assume someone else will respond.
The elimination of responsibility once an issue has received media coverage.

questions.explanation: The article describes diffusion of responsibility: awareness can coexist with inaction when people expect somebody else to respond.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 1 — Penneys: ethics–price paradox; assigned week(s): 2

questions.stem: The Penneys reading discusses continued commercial success alongside public concern about production conditions. Which ONE of the following conclusions would NOT be justified by continued sales alone?

options.text: Public controversy and commercial growth can occur during the same period.
A boycott may attract attention without producing a lasting fall in purchases.
Price may remain important to customers who have heard ethical criticisms.
Customers have positively verified that every supplier meets acceptable labour standards.
Purchasing behaviour can differ from publicly expressed ethical concern.

questions.explanation: Sales reveal purchasing behaviour, not proof that customers have verified every supplier or that all labour concerns have been resolved.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 1 — Penneys: ethics–price paradox; assigned week(s): 2

questions.stem: With reference to the Penneys article, a retailer points to jobs created and its supplier code as a complete answer to concerns about factory conditions. Which ONE of the following is the strongest evaluation?

options.text: Employment benefits establish that all supplier practices are acceptable.
The existence of any supplier code establishes that all reported abuses occurred.
Employment benefits and a code are relevant, but neither alone establishes actual conditions or resolves the concerns.
Consumer demand makes the retailer unable to influence purchasing arrangements.
A written code removes the need to examine how production actually occurs.

questions.explanation: The article contrasts ethical assurances and the benefits of employment with concerns about actual production. Relevant benefits and policies are not substitutes for evidence of implementation.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 1 — Penneys: ethics–price paradox; assigned week(s): 2

questions.stem: According to the prescribed Milgram reading, which ONE of the following statements about the classic experimental condition is TRUE?

options.text: Every participant stopped as soon as the learner first objected.
The results were unaffected by changes to the experimental situation.
About 65% continued to the maximum labelled 450 volts, although the shocks were not real.
The study compared only people already known to have violent criminal records.
About 65% knowingly administered real 450-volt shocks to another participant.

questions.explanation: The reading describes about 65% reaching the maximum labelled voltage in the classic condition. The learner was not receiving real shocks.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 2 — The Milgram Shock Experiment

questions.stem: According to the prescribed Milgram reading, why are variations involving the learner’s proximity, other participants and the setting important?

options.text: They establish that the shocks became real in the later conditions.
They establish that no participant understood the experimental instructions.
They remove the need to consider authority when interpreting obedience.
They show why every participant must have possessed the same personality.
They demonstrate that situational conditions can affect how far participants continue.

questions.explanation: The reading describes experimental variations that altered situational pressures and obedience, rather than treating behaviour as fixed solely by personality.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 2 — The Milgram Shock Experiment; assigned week(s): 2

questions.stem: In the Milgram reading, “engaged followership” offers an interpretation of participants’ behaviour. Which ONE of the following most accurately describes that interpretation?

options.text: Participants obey only because an actual legal penalty is threatened.
Participants’ behaviour demonstrates that group identification cannot matter.
Participants continue only after personally verifying that the learner is unharmed.
Participants may identify with the leader’s scientific cause and actively support it.
Participants have no understanding of the purpose presented to them.

questions.explanation: Engaged followership stresses identification with the experimenter’s cause, rather than explaining obedience exclusively as mindless submission.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 2 — The Milgram Shock Experiment; assigned week(s): 2

questions.stem: With reference to the ethical evaluation of Milgram’s research in the assigned reading, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.text: The lack of real shocks means that participants could not experience distress.
The absence of real shocks does not eliminate concerns about deception and psychological stress.
Participants’ visible distress proves that all of them stopped immediately.
A participant’s agreement to enter the study removes every subsequent ethical concern.
Scientific interest alone settles whether deception is ethically acceptable.

questions.explanation: The learner did not receive real shocks, but participants believed otherwise. Deception and experienced distress remain relevant to evaluating the research.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 2 — The Milgram Shock Experiment; assigned week(s): 2

chapters.title: Week 3 — Business Environment
chapters.description: Reading allocation follows the module outline; lecture questions retain delivered-week placement. Five options; single answer; AI-written practice.

questions.stem: With reference to the economic indicators used in the Week 3 material, which ONE of the following statements correctly distinguishes GDP from GDP per capita?

options.text: GDP and GDP per capita both show the disposable income received by each household.
GDP measures total output; GDP per capita expresses output per person.
GDP per capita removes the need to consider population size when interpreting living standards.
GDP per capita measures how equally output is distributed within the population.
GDP measures average personal wellbeing; GDP per capita measures total national wealth.

questions.explanation: GDP is aggregate output, while GDP per capita divides output by population. Neither figure alone shows how income or wellbeing is distributed.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 3 — The World Around Us and the Impact of Business

questions.stem: A student compares the annual number of road deaths with the annual number of aviation deaths and uses the totals to state how much riskier a single journey is in one form of transport. Which ONE of the following is needed before that particular conclusion can be justified?

options.text: Comparable measures of exposure, such as journeys or distance travelled.
The land area of the countries in which the deaths occurred.
A ranking of the two industries by their contribution to GDP.
The assumption that every reported transport death receives equal publicity.
A common currency in which to express the two death totals.

questions.explanation: Raw death totals do not establish per-journey risk. Comparable exposure denominators are needed before forming a risk ratio.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 3 — The World Around Us and the Impact of Business

questions.stem: With reference to the Rubaya coltan example in the Week 3 material, which ONE of the following most accurately identifies the business-ethics issue illustrated?

options.text: Connections between electronic inputs, conflict financing and conditions in mineral supply chains.
The view that conflict is relevant only where the final customer directly funds an armed group.
The claim that a useful final product establishes the acceptability of its production conditions.
The claim that every finished electronic device has an identical mineral supply chain.
The view that responsibility for mineral sourcing ends when materials leave the mine.

questions.explanation: The coltan example connects mineral inputs with conflict funding and worker conditions. It does not prove that every electronic device has the same origin.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 3 — The World Around Us and the Impact of Business

questions.stem: One report measures food waste in Europe in tonnes. Another estimates the monetary value of wasted food in the United States. A student adds the two numerical figures and presents the result as a global food-waste total. Which ONE of the following statements about this calculation is TRUE?

options.text: The two figures establish a current global total because they concern the same issue.
The higher numerical figure necessarily identifies the region wasting more food.
The monetary estimate can be treated as a tonnage estimate once both figures are rounded.
The figures are comparable without adjustment if both reports describe waste as significant.
The figures cannot simply be added because their units and geographical scopes differ.

questions.explanation: Tonnes and financial values measure different things, and European and US figures have different scopes; they cannot simply be summed.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 3 — The World Around Us and the Impact of Business

questions.stem: The Week 3 material places examples of luxury consumption alongside examples of homelessness and deprivation. Which ONE of the following interpretations is best supported by that contrast, without adding an unsupported causal claim?

options.text: A direct causal link between each luxury purchase and a particular person’s homelessness.
Unequal access to resources and security despite the presence of substantial wealth.
The inference that every affluent consumer has breached the same legal obligation.
The inference that housing insecurity can be explained solely by personal spending decisions.
The claim that total economic growth ensures equivalent security for every household.

questions.explanation: The contrast concerns the distribution of resources and security. It does not establish that each affluent person caused a particular case of homelessness.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 3 — The World Around Us and the Impact of Business

questions.stem: During a drought, an industrial beverage producer continues to use water while residents experience difficulty obtaining supplies for everyday needs. The producer points to jobs and revenue as reasons why its position should prevail. Which ONE of the following identifies the central issue that an ethical analysis must still address?

options.text: The view that employment benefits settle all questions about access to water.
The competing claims of businesses and communities over a scarce essential resource.
The view that water allocation becomes an ethical issue only after a company breaks the law.
The presumption that household use must be ignored because it does not produce a market return.
The presumption that commercial use has priority whenever it produces measurable revenue.

questions.explanation: Water is essential and scarce in the example, so company activity must be considered alongside residents’ claims rather than through revenue alone.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 3 — The World Around Us and the Impact of Business

questions.stem: With reference to the interpretation of ocean-plastics estimates, which ONE of the following would be INCORRECT?

options.text: Checking the geographical scope and measurement method.
Distinguishing a stock of pollution from a flow of additional pollution.
Treating an estimate of accumulated plastic as if it were the amount entering the ocean each year.
Checking the year in which the estimate was made.
Distinguishing estimates of plastic on the ocean floor from estimates at the surface.

questions.explanation: A stock measures accumulated material, while a flow measures additions over a period. Treating one as the other changes the meaning of the estimate.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 3 — The World Around Us and the Impact of Business

questions.stem: With reference to the Purdue Pharma report included in the Week 3 material, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE without treating allegations or historical reporting as a complete account of all later legal outcomes?

options.text: The case establishes that all medicines create the same addiction risks.
The 2019 report describes bankruptcy amid allegations of downplaying OxyContin’s addiction risks.
The filing removes the need to distinguish reported allegations from established findings.
The report provides a complete account of every subsequent legal outcome.
The bankruptcy report itself proves every allegation made in all related litigation.

questions.explanation: The source is a 2019 report about bankruptcy amid allegations. Neither the filing nor that article supplies a complete adjudication or all subsequent outcomes.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 3 — The World Around Us and the Impact of Business

questions.stem: With reference to the maps and population comparisons in the Week 3 material, which ONE of the following statements is FALSE?

options.text: The quantity represented should be checked before using visual size in an argument.
A map may represent physical area rather than population.
Projection and presentation can affect impressions of relative size.
Population and economic output are different measures.
A country that appears larger on a map necessarily has a larger population and a larger consumer market.

questions.explanation: Visual area is not a population measure. The represented quantity and presentation must be checked before drawing a market-size conclusion.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 3 — The World Around Us and the Impact of Business

questions.stem: A chart of recorded crime and a survey of the public’s fear of crime appear to move in different directions. With reference to the Week 3 discussion of perception and evidence, which ONE of the following is TRUE?

options.text: A recorded trend makes perceptions irrelevant to the effects on people’s lives.
They can measure different things, so the definitions, periods and claims should be checked before assuming that one is false.
A strong public perception automatically establishes the corresponding crime rate.
Two measures concerning the same topic must always move together.
The difference proves that the survey respondents fabricated their answers.

questions.explanation: Recorded events and perceptions are not identical quantities. Divergence requires careful interpretation, not an automatic accusation or causal conclusion.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 3 — The World Around Us and the Impact of Business

questions.stem: With reference to the Costa Coffee example in the supplied Week 3 material, which ONE of the following is TRUE?

options.text: The example concerns lobbying against a proposed UK levy on single-use cups, rather than proof that the proposed levy was already in force.
The article establishes a current legal ban on every disposable cup.
Opposition to a proposed levy is equivalent to a court finding that the company evaded an existing tax.
The example shows that lobbying has no connection with environmental policy.
The presence of a company policy establishes that all packaging-waste effects have been eliminated.

questions.explanation: The source describes lobbying about a proposed measure. A proposal, political activity and an enacted legal obligation should not be conflated.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 3 — The World Around Us and the Impact of Business

questions.stem: With reference to the Amazon example in the Week 3 material, which ONE of the following best describes an environmental tipping-point concern?

options.text: Environmental consequences can be assessed only by measuring a company’s current profit.
A reported tipping-point risk establishes that the entire rainforest has already disappeared.
Sufficient stress may move an ecosystem towards a different state, rather than simply producing a small reversible change of the same kind.
Every additional environmental pressure must have an identical and easily reversible effect.
An ecosystem cannot change its functioning unless a company is first convicted of an offence.

questions.explanation: The rainforest-to-savannah example concerns a possible change of ecosystem state; a warning about risk is not proof that every part of the forest has already changed.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 3 — The World Around Us and the Impact of Business

questions.stem: With reference to the core reading on woke-washing and social-purpose branding, which ONE of the following is the most appropriate way to assess a company’s ethical claims?

options.text: Assess only whether the slogan attracts attention, rather than what the firm does.
Treat criticism of a campaign as proof that its stated social goal is undesirable.
Treat a progressive campaign as sufficient proof that the firm’s operations are ethical.
Compare a firm’s social-purpose message with its labour, supply-chain and other substantive practices.
Assume that every social-purpose campaign is insincere without examining evidence.

questions.explanation: The woke-washing critique tests whether stated social commitments match operations; neither accepting slogans nor rejecting every campaign without evidence is sufficient.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 3 — Woke-washing and culture-war branding

questions.stem: In Owen Jones’s critique of woke-washing, a branded campaign makes a donation to a worthwhile organisation. Which ONE of the following best preserves the distinction made in the article?

options.text: A worthwhile recipient makes scrutiny of the donor’s conduct inappropriate.
Commercial motivation means that the recipient cannot obtain any benefit.
A donation proves that the company has resolved all concerns about its employment practices.
A donation can benefit its recipient while the campaign’s wider corporate purpose remains open to criticism.
The amount donated establishes that every consumer shares the campaign’s values.

questions.explanation: Jones recognises that a donation can have a useful effect while questioning the alignment between progressive branding and corporate conduct.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 3 — Woke-washing and culture-war branding; assigned week(s): 3

questions.stem: A company responds to criticism of its working conditions by pointing to a highly visible social-purpose campaign. According to the woke-washing reading, which ONE of the following would provide the most relevant further evidence?

options.text: Whether the campaign allows consumers to display the brand prominently.
The number of colours used on the company’s packaging.
Whether the campaign has received more publicity than competitors’ campaigns.
Whether employment and supply-chain practices are consistent with the advertised commitment.
The popularity of the campaign’s slogan considered on its own.

questions.explanation: The critique concerns the relationship between symbolic positioning and substantive conduct. Evidence about actual practices is more probative than visibility alone.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 3 — Woke-washing and culture-war branding; assigned week(s): 3

questions.stem: With reference to the woke-washing article, which ONE of the following statements is FALSE?

options.text: A progressive advertising message is sufficient evidence of an ethical business model.
A social issue can become a source of brand differentiation and publicity.
The conduct behind a campaign can be examined separately from the attractiveness of its message.
A company can communicate progressive values while retaining practices that conflict with them.
A useful donation does not settle every criticism of its corporate sponsor.

questions.explanation: Progressive messaging alone is not sufficient evidence of an ethical business model; this gap is central to the article’s critique.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 3 — Woke-washing and culture-war branding; assigned week(s): 3

questions.stem: According to the organisational analysis in Reading 4, which ONE of the following should accompany an examination of individual employees’ decisions in the Wells Fargo example?

options.text: A conclusion that applying a named ethical theory removes the need for case evidence.
A presumption that commercial success validates the practices used to achieve it.
A focus on external advertising while excluding internal targets.
Examination of managerial pressures, incentives and organisational culture.
An assumption that all employee decisions are isolated from the organisation.

questions.explanation: The Wells Fargo discussion connects individual decisions with targets, managerial pressure and organisational culture, rather than treating them as isolated choices.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 4 — Evaluating business ethics in practice

questions.stem: In the Wells Fargo example discussed in Reading 4, which ONE of the following most accurately identifies the relationship between sales targets and misconduct?

options.text: Organisational targets are irrelevant because only the final individual action can be examined.
Cross-selling targets demonstrate that every customer freely requested the additional accounts.
Cross-selling pressure is relevant to understanding why employees opened accounts without customers’ authorisation.
The presence of targets makes the accounts authorised even where customers did not consent.
Customer consent can be inferred from the bank’s internal recording of a sale.

questions.explanation: The reading links unauthorised accounts to organisational sales pressures. Explaining that context does not turn the accounts into authorised transactions.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 4 — Evaluating business ethics in practice; assigned week(s): 3

questions.stem: According to Reading 4’s organisational analysis, why is a strategy of simply recruiting exceptionally moral employees an incomplete response to misconduct?

options.text: An ethical organisation must dispense with all performance expectations.
Recruitment alone does not address incentives, managerial constraints and organisational culture.
Employees cannot recognise an ethical problem until a court rules on it.
Any misconduct proves that an organisation has no written policies.
Individual judgement never matters in business decisions.

questions.explanation: The source questions reliance on unusually virtuous individuals while leaving organisational conditions unchanged. Incentives and culture also require attention.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 4 — Evaluating business ethics in practice; assigned week(s): 3

questions.stem: A bank dismisses several employees following unauthorised sales but leaves its targets, rewards and managerial expectations unchanged. With reference to Reading 4, which ONE of the following is the most appropriate concern?

options.text: The response may leave organisational pressures that encouraged the misconduct in place.
Customer authorisation becomes irrelevant once disciplinary action has occurred.
The bank must choose between investigating individuals and investigating management.
Dismissing employees establishes that the underlying causes have been removed.
Any change in staffing necessarily changes the organisation’s culture.

questions.explanation: An individual-only response can miss continuing organisational conditions. The reading supports examining both employees’ conduct and the system shaping it.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 4 — Evaluating business ethics in practice; assigned week(s): 3

chapters.title: Week 4 — Ethical Frameworks (1)
chapters.description: Reading allocation follows the module outline; lecture questions retain delivered-week placement. Reading 6 also revisited in Week 5. Five options; single answer; AI-written practice.

questions.stem: With reference to the different approaches to studying ethics, which ONE of the following pairings is correct?

options.text: Conceptual ethics: measuring profit; descriptive ethics: prescribing duties.
Descriptive ethics: defining moral terms; normative ethics: recording preferences without evaluating them.
Descriptive ethics: what people do; normative ethics: what people ought to do.
Normative ethics: collecting behaviour data without value judgements; conceptual ethics: predicting sales.
Descriptive ethics: what people ought to do; normative ethics: what they actually do.

questions.explanation: Descriptive ethics describes conduct; normative ethics evaluates what ought to be done. The distinction is between observation and prescription.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 1 — Introduction to Ethical Theories and Frameworks

questions.stem: Two managers agree that deliberately misleading customers is wrong. They disagree about a particular advertisement because one thinks its wording is misleading and the other does not. Which ONE of the following best identifies the distinction that should be made before concluding that they hold different moral standards?

options.text: Disagreement about the facts or their application need not be disagreement about the moral standard.
The disagreement can be resolved without examining the wording or context of the statement.
Only the number of people supporting each judgement matters once a standard is agreed.
Disagreement about a judgement necessarily proves that neither person accepts a moral standard.
Agreement on a standard guarantees agreement about every case to which it applies.

questions.explanation: People can share a principle but disagree about facts or how it applies. Clarifying the evidence may therefore matter more than changing the standard.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 1 — Introduction to Ethical Theories and Frameworks

questions.stem: A practice is widely accepted in a country in which a company operates. With reference to the discussion of ethical relativism, which ONE of the following conclusions does NOT follow merely from that fact?

options.text: Cultural context may be relevant when understanding the practice.
An ethical analysis may need to distinguish acceptance from justification.
People from different contexts may initially judge the practice differently.
The practice may influence what people expect others to do.
The practice is therefore morally acceptable.

questions.explanation: The fact that a practice is common describes social acceptance; it does not independently justify that practice morally.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 1 — Introduction to Ethical Theories and Frameworks

questions.stem: Which option gives the COMPLETE set of consequentialist ethical theories among those listed below?

options.text: Utilitarianism.
Ethical egoism.
Kantian deontology.
a) and b) above.
a), b) and c) above.

questions.explanation: Utilitarianism and ethical egoism assess consequences, though they focus on different beneficiaries. Kantian deontology gives priority to duty rather than consequence totals.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 1 — Introduction to Ethical Theories and Frameworks; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 2 — Utilitarianism; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 3 — Egoism

questions.stem: With reference to utilitarianism as discussed in the module, which ONE of the following statements correctly distinguishes act utilitarianism from rule utilitarianism?

options.text: Act utilitarianism evaluates motives; rule utilitarianism evaluates character traits.
Act utilitarianism protects shareholders; rule utilitarianism gives priority to employees.
Act utilitarianism considers consequences; rule utilitarianism excludes consequences from its justification.
Act utilitarianism maximises personal gain; rule utilitarianism follows duties regardless of outcomes.
Act utilitarianism evaluates a particular action; rule utilitarianism considers the consequences of generally following a rule.

questions.explanation: Act utilitarianism examines a particular decision, while rule utilitarianism considers the consequences of generally adopting a rule.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 2 — Utilitarianism

questions.stem: A proposed development would produce substantial aggregate benefits, but a small community would bear serious losses. A manager argues that the large total benefit makes the community’s objections irrelevant. Which ONE of the following identifies a recognised difficulty with that argument?

options.text: The interests of a minority must be excluded from a utilitarian calculation.
Aggregate gains can obscure the distribution of burdens and leave a minority seriously disadvantaged.
Only harms that can be expressed in money are eligible for ethical consideration.
The project must be rejected without comparing any alternative outcomes.
Benefits to more people establish that no individual rights have been affected.

questions.explanation: A positive aggregate result can coexist with severe minority losses. Distribution remains a significant difficulty for a simple total-benefit calculation.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 2 — Utilitarianism

questions.stem: A company gives monetary values to employment, illness, environmental damage and other effects of a project, and then compares the resulting total with the totals for alternative projects. With reference to the lecture’s critique of utilitarian calculation, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.text: A positive financial return to the company is equivalent to a positive result for all affected people.
The use of numbers removes the need to justify the selected measures.
Environmental damage cannot enter an analysis of consequences.
The result depends partly on contested judgements about what to count and how to value it.
Comparing alternatives is unnecessary once one option has some benefits.

questions.explanation: Cost–benefit results depend on which effects are included and how they are valued; numerical presentation does not remove those judgements.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 2 — Utilitarianism

questions.stem: According to Mill’s harm principle, as discussed in the module and the prescribed textbook reading, which ONE of the following is the most appropriate objection to coercing an adult solely to protect that adult from a self-regarding choice?

options.text: Coercion is justified whenever the majority believes an individual’s choice is unwise.
The principle requires adding up every private benefit before considering individual liberty.
The principle permits coercion only after harm has actually occurred, never to prevent it.
Preventing harm to others, rather than merely benefiting the individual, is the relevant justification for coercion against their will.
Any expected benefit to the individual is sufficient to justify coercion.

questions.explanation: Mill’s harm principle distinguishes preventing harm to others from coercing an adult merely for that adult’s own good.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 2 — Utilitarianism; Reading 5 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 44–53)

questions.stem: With reference to the distinction between immediate desire and enlightened self-interest, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.text: It treats every short-term commercial opportunity as equally worthwhile.
It requires abandoning the decision-maker’s interests in every case.
It judges actions by duty regardless of their consequences.
It requires equal financial returns for every affected stakeholder.
It takes a longer-term view of the decision-maker’s interests.

questions.explanation: Enlightened egoism considers longer-term self-interest, which can favour foregoing immediate gains to preserve valuable relationships or opportunities.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 3 — Egoism

questions.stem: In the kidney-sale dilemma discussed in class, a person in severe poverty agrees to sell a kidney for payment. Which ONE of the following best explains why the fact of stated consent does not, by itself, settle the ethical issue?

options.text: Poverty, possible deception and lasting injury affect the context and consequences of the choice.
Personal ownership eliminates every further question about duties or fairness.
The recipient’s expected benefit removes the need to assess the seller’s circumstances.
A payment automatically makes a bodily transaction morally acceptable.
Consent is relevant only where the seller receives no payment.

questions.explanation: Consent must be considered in context. Poverty, misinformation and lasting injury can raise ethical concerns even where a transaction is formally accepted.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 3 — Egoism

questions.stem: With reference to a utilitarian assessment of a proposed factory, which option gives the COMPLETE set of relevant consequences below?

options.text: Benefits such as employment and the goods produced.
Harms such as illness and environmental damage.
The likely consequences of feasible alternatives, rather than the proposal alone.
a) and b) above.
a), b) and c) above.

questions.explanation: Utilitarian comparison concerns the balance of benefits and harms across realistic alternatives, not simply the advantages of the chosen proposal.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 2 — Utilitarianism

questions.stem: A company forgoes a short-term saving because it expects that fair treatment of customers will protect repeat business and long-term revenue. Which ONE of the following statements about this reasoning is TRUE?

options.text: It must be a Kantian motive because the outcome benefits someone other than the company.
It establishes that customers have been considered solely as ends, independently of the company’s return.
It can be an example of enlightened self-interest even though the action also benefits customers.
It shows that commercial advantage and responsible conduct can never occur together.
It cannot be egoist reasoning because it gives up an immediate gain.

questions.explanation: Enlightened self-interest can take a long-term commercial view and produce benefits for others without being identical to acting from duty.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 3 — Egoism; Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: With reference to the prescribed OpenStax reading on Bentham, Mill and Kant, which ONE of the following correctly distinguishes utilitarian from Kantian reasoning?

options.text: The two approaches differ only in terminology and must recommend the same action.
Kantian reasoning treats a profitable result as sufficient to establish a duty-based motive.
Both approaches define the right action solely by the executive’s private financial return.
Utilitarianism excludes the consequences for people other than the decision-maker.
Utilitarianism assesses consequences for overall utility; Kantian reasoning gives a central role to duty and the basis of action.

questions.explanation: Utilitarian reasoning centres on overall consequences; Kantian reasoning centres on duty and the basis of action. The two need not give identical recommendations.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 5 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 44–53)

questions.stem: According to the prescribed OpenStax discussion of Bentham, which ONE of the following best describes the attraction of a single numerical index of utility?

options.text: It establishes that every person experiences the same pleasure from every good.
It allows motives to replace consequences as the only basis of judgement.
It removes the need to consider anyone outside the company making a decision.
It makes legal compliance the definition of utility.
It promises a common basis for comparing the pleasure and pain associated with alternatives.

questions.explanation: Bentham sought a common numerical measure of utility. The ambition to compare effects does not establish that measurement is effortless or experiences identical.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 5 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 44–53); assigned week(s): 4

questions.stem: With reference to the OpenStax account of Mill, which ONE of the following is TRUE?

options.text: Mill’s account makes the avoidance of all disagreement the purpose of social policy.
Freedom matters only where it directly increases an employer’s income.
A person’s flourishing can be reduced to the company’s profit for the current period.
Individual development is irrelevant once total commercial output increases.
Mill treats individual development and liberty as important rather than describing people solely as passive recipients of pleasure.

questions.explanation: The reading contrasts a narrowly mechanical utility calculation with Mill’s concern for individual development, liberty and human flourishing.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 5 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 44–53); assigned week(s): 4

questions.stem: A manager says, “I will judge the policy by its consequences; whether I act from duty is a different question.” With reference to Reading 5, which ONE of the following is the best interpretation?

options.text: The manager has shown that utilitarian and Kantian reasoning use identical criteria.
The manager has established that every duty must be conditional on profit.
The manager has replaced ethical reasoning with a purely descriptive account of current practice.
The manager has distinguished an outcome-based assessment from a duty-based assessment of moral motivation.
The manager has demonstrated that an outcome-based assessment cannot include harms.

questions.explanation: Reading 5 distinguishes assessment by consequences from Kantian attention to duty and motives. Recognising the distinction does not itself resolve which approach should prevail.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 5 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 44–53); assigned week(s): 4

questions.stem: In the Rawls reading, consider a person who divides a cake without knowing which slice they will receive. Which ONE of the following features of fair decision-making is illustrated by this arrangement?

options.text: Existing property holdings determine the only permissible principles of distribution.
Equal basic liberties must be traded away whenever aggregate output increases.
Fairness can be assessed without considering how the decision affects different positions.
The divider should first secure the largest share and then justify the allocation.
Not knowing one’s eventual position can discourage designing the arrangement solely for personal advantage.

questions.explanation: Uncertainty about which share one receives can discourage self-serving allocation and illustrates the logic of impartial choice.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 6 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 54–58)

questions.stem: According to the OpenStax account of Nozick’s objection to Rawls, which ONE of the following most accurately identifies the dispute?

options.text: Whether firms should calculate profits before paying wages.
Whether a voluntary donation is impossible in a market economy.
Whether all differences in preferences should be eliminated by law.
Whether impartial reasoning requires decision-makers to know their own future income.
Whether a state may redistribute property that people have legally acquired or inherited.

questions.explanation: The reading presents Nozick’s entitlement-based objection to the state’s redistribution of legally acquired or inherited property.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 6 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 54–58); assigned week(s): 4, 5

questions.stem: A group is choosing social principles. Each member knows their own wealth and selects whichever rule will favour their existing position. According to Reading 6, which ONE of the following features of Rawls’s method is missing?

options.text: The instruction to maximise only the richest member’s utility.
The assumption that present advantages establish moral entitlement to future advantages.
The requirement that everyone have exactly the same personal preferences.
The removal of information about one’s own social position when selecting principles.
The use of current market power to determine who may participate.

questions.explanation: The veil of ignorance removes knowledge of one’s particular position so that principles are not simply selected to protect existing personal advantages.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 6 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 54–58); assigned week(s): 4, 5

questions.stem: With reference to Rawls’s criticism of utilitarianism in the prescribed reading, which ONE of the following is the central concern?

options.text: Justice can be determined by taking a poll of the wealthiest citizens.
A calculation of aggregate utility may permit some people’s interests or freedoms to be sacrificed for a larger total.
Any consideration of other people’s welfare is necessarily unjust.
Impartial principles become unnecessary once all effects are given monetary values.
An unequal distribution is justified whenever its beneficiaries approve it.

questions.explanation: The reading questions whether aggregate utility adequately protects persons and justice, including the risk of sacrificing some people’s interests for others’ gains.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 6 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 54–58); assigned week(s): 4, 5

chapters.title: Week 5 — Ethical Frameworks (2)
chapters.description: Reading allocation follows the module outline; lecture questions retain delivered-week placement. Reading 7 also revisited in Week 6. Five options; single answer; AI-written practice.

questions.stem: According to Kant’s universal-law formulation, which ONE of the following questions should be asked when evaluating the maxim on which a person proposes to act?

options.text: Would the action strengthen a character trait admired by the decision-maker’s colleagues?
Would the action advance the decision-maker’s long-term commercial interest?
Would the action produce the greatest net benefit in this particular case?
Could the maxim of the action be willed as a universal law without reserving an exception for oneself?
Would most customers approve of the action in an opinion poll?

questions.explanation: The universal-law test asks whether one could consistently will the action’s maxim as a general law without a special exception for oneself.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 1 — Kantian Ethics

questions.stem: A retailer tells staff that they should be honest because customers will eventually discover deception and take their business elsewhere. Honesty is supported only for as long as it remains commercially advantageous. With reference to the Kantian account in the module, this motive is best described as which ONE of the following?

options.text: Prudential conduct motivated by commercial advantage, rather than honesty from duty.
An example of a negative right that settles the owner’s motive.
A universal moral requirement derived from the owner’s expected profit.
Conduct from duty because it has the same outward appearance as duty-based honesty.
Virtuous conduct solely because customers benefit from the transaction.

questions.explanation: Honesty motivated only by commercial advantage is prudential. Its outward result does not establish that the person acted from duty.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 1 — Kantian Ethics

questions.stem: A person freely agrees to a fair employment relationship and is treated with dignity. The employer benefits from the person’s skills and the employee benefits from the exchange. With reference to Kant’s instruction not to treat people “merely” as means, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.text: An employment contract establishes that no later unfair treatment is possible.
Every use of another person’s skills is forbidden, even with consent and fair treatment.
Payment removes the need to respect the person’s independent purposes.
Using another person’s skills in a mutually beneficial relationship need not reduce that person to a mere instrument.
A mutually beneficial outcome excuses any deception used to obtain the person’s consent.

questions.explanation: The qualification “merely” allows cooperation and mutually beneficial use of skills while requiring respect for people’s own purposes and dignity.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 1 — Kantian Ethics

questions.stem: With reference to the criticisms of duty-based ethics discussed in the module, which ONE of the following is a recognised difficulty?

options.text: It defines the right action only as the action with the greatest aggregate benefit.
Duties can conflict, leaving difficult questions about what to do in a particular situation.
It has no way to distinguish a duty-based motive from a commercial motive.
It requires treating every social convention as a universal moral law.
It treats a person’s dignity as irrelevant whenever a majority gains.
