questions.explanation: Duty-based approaches can encounter conflicting obligations. Identifying duties does not automatically determine how every conflict should be resolved.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 1 — Kantian Ethics

questions.stem: According to the virtue-ethics approach discussed in the module, which ONE of the following should be the central focus of ethical development?

options.text: The cultivation of character through recurring patterns of conduct.
The enforceability of a contract as the sole test of good conduct.
The likelihood that an action will escape punishment.
The net consequences of each isolated act as the only moral criterion.
The satisfaction of whatever preferences a person happens to have.

questions.explanation: Virtue ethics focuses on cultivated character and recurring conduct, rather than reducing morality to the result of an isolated act.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 2 — Virtue Ethics

questions.stem: Which ONE of the following pairs most clearly represents moral virtues, rather than commercial strength or performance alone?

options.text: Integrity and compassion.
Ambition and bargaining power.
Visibility and popularity.
Aggressiveness and dominance.
Market share and sales growth.

questions.explanation: Integrity and compassion are moral qualities, whereas market share and dominance are not themselves sufficient evidence of virtue.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 2 — Virtue Ethics

questions.stem: An organisation’s code praises courage, honesty and compassion. In a difficult case, staff agree that these are desirable qualities but still disagree about which action should be taken. Which ONE of the following limitations of a virtue-based approach is illustrated?

options.text: Identifying desirable character traits may not provide a precise decision procedure for every case.
A virtuous person must give identical answers to every moral dilemma.
An action has moral worth only when it is required by an employment contract.
Virtue ethics is concerned only with financial outcomes.
Character cannot be developed through repeated behaviour.

questions.explanation: A list of virtues can orient judgement without providing an exact procedure for resolving every difficult choice.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 2 — Virtue Ethics

questions.stem: With reference to rights theories, which ONE of the following statements correctly distinguishes positive rights from negative rights?

options.text: Positive rights are always legally enforceable; negative rights are always voluntary.
Positive rights belong to employees; negative rights belong to employers.
Positive rights concern money; negative rights can never create obligations.
Positive rights require provision or action; negative rights require non-interference.
Positive rights are moral claims; negative rights are necessarily unlawful claims.

questions.explanation: Positive rights call for action or provision, while negative rights call for others to refrain from interference. Both can imply duties.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences

questions.stem: With reference to Rawls’s original position and veil of ignorance, which ONE of the following best describes the purpose of the exercise?

options.text: To choose principles without knowing the social position one will occupy.
To eliminate every possible difference in personal outcomes.
To choose principles after confirming that one will belong to the wealthiest group.
To choose principles using only the preferences of existing property owners.
To replace equal liberties with whichever allocation produces the highest GDP.

questions.explanation: The veil of ignorance removes knowledge of one’s eventual social position so that principles are not chosen simply to favour a known personal advantage.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences; Reading 6 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 54–58)

questions.stem: According to the difference principle discussed in the module, which ONE of the following justifications for an economic inequality is LEAST consistent with the principle?

options.text: A proposed inequality should be assessed partly by its implications for the least advantaged.
Assessing inequality requires more than identifying who produces the largest private return.
The distribution of gains matters, not merely the size of the total gain.
Equal division of every reward is not the only conceivable just arrangement.
An inequality is justified simply because total output rises, even though the least advantaged receive no benefit.

questions.explanation: The difference principle cannot justify inequality merely by pointing to aggregate growth while the least advantaged receive no benefit.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences; Reading 6 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 54–58)

questions.stem: A company invites stakeholders to a consultation but allows the largest investor to determine the outcome. Residents who will bear some of the effects are present but cannot meaningfully contribute. With reference to discourse ethics, which ONE of the following is the most relevant criticism?

options.text: Dialogue is ethically satisfactory once the most powerful party agrees.
Consensus requires excluding participants whose concerns are difficult to measure.
The process should consider only stakeholders with contractual voting rights.
The conditions for genuine dialogue are undermined when power dominates participation.
Participation removes the need to give reasons for a decision.

questions.explanation: Discourse ethics requires meaningful participation and reason-giving; domination by power undermines the conditions of genuine dialogue.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences

questions.stem: With reference to the lecture’s discussion of resolving moral disagreements, which option gives the COMPLETE set of useful steps below?

options.text: Clarifying the facts about which people disagree.
Clarifying the meanings of important terms.
Checking the consistency of the reasons being offered.
a) and b) above.
a), b) and c) above.

questions.explanation: Clarifying facts, meanings and consistency addresses different sources of disagreement, so all three steps are relevant.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences

questions.stem: With reference to Kantian ethics as discussed in the module, which ONE of the following statements is FALSE?

options.text: Respectful cooperation need not be prohibited simply because people benefit from one another’s skills.
An exception reserved for oneself can undermine a proposed universal rule.
The motive of duty differs from acting only because honesty is commercially useful.
An action that benefits the majority is justified even if it deliberately treats a minority merely as instruments.
The maxim of an action should be tested for universalisation.

questions.explanation: Kant’s humanity formulation does not permit reducing people to mere instruments simply by pointing to an aggregate gain.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 1 — Kantian Ethics

questions.stem: With reference to virtue ethics, which ONE of the following statements is FALSE?

options.text: A single commercially successful act establishes that a person has a virtuous character, regardless of their recurring conduct.
Character is developed through repeated practice and habits.
Relationships can be relevant to the development and expression of character.
Identifying a virtue does not remove every need for practical judgement.
Integrity and compassion are not equivalent to market dominance.

questions.explanation: Virtue ethics examines cultivated character and patterns of conduct. Neither isolated success nor a single good act settles the whole assessment.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 2 — Virtue Ethics

questions.stem: With reference to Rawls’s account of justice in the assigned material, which option gives the COMPLETE set of relevant principles below?

options.text: Equal basic liberties.
Fair equality of opportunity.
Attention to the position of the least advantaged when assessing inequality.
a) and b) above.
a), b) and c) above.

questions.explanation: The material distinguishes basic liberty, fair opportunity and the position of the least advantaged rather than reducing justice to aggregate wealth.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences; Reading 6 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 54–58)

questions.stem: With reference to discourse ethics, which ONE of the following would NOT support the conditions for a meaningful stakeholder dialogue?

options.text: Recognising the time and inclusion difficulties involved in seeking agreement.
Offering reasons that other participants can examine.
Making it possible for affected groups to contribute.
Allowing the strongest participant to settle the outcome without considering the reasons offered by others.
Considering whether differences in power prevent genuine participation.

questions.explanation: Dialogue is undermined when power determines the outcome without meaningful participation and consideration of reasons.
questions.source: AI-written practice; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences

questions.stem: According to Robert Reich’s critique in the core CSR reading, which ONE of the following best explains why voluntary corporate promises may not be a sufficient response to social problems?

options.text: Profit incentives can constrain voluntary corporate promises, making enforceable rules and penalties important.
Every profitable social initiative necessarily demonstrates that regulation is unnecessary.
Voluntary promises remove the need for democratic regulation and enforcement.
The existence of a public commitment establishes that a company will bear any cost to fulfil it.
Corporate leaders can always solve social problems without changing the incentives they face.

questions.explanation: Reich argues that voluntary CSR is constrained by profit incentives, which is why enforceable rules and penalties matter in his critique.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 7 — Why Corporate Social Responsibility is BS

questions.stem: In Robert Reich’s CSR article, why does the relationship between the likely cost of penalties and the profit from misconduct matter?

options.text: The possibility of punishment guarantees that all firms comply voluntarily.
A company is ethically entitled to break a law whenever the expected penalty is low.
A penalty removes every incentive to break a rule regardless of its size or enforcement.
Profit incentives cease to operate once a company signs a public pledge.
Weak enforcement and low expected penalties can leave misconduct commercially attractive.

questions.explanation: Reich’s argument concerns incentives: expected consequences of enforcement must matter relative to gains. This explains a risk; it is not an ethical permission to break the law.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 7 — Why Corporate Social Responsibility is BS; assigned week(s): 5, 6

questions.stem: According to Reich’s article, a business group publicly supports stakeholders but opposes tax measures that could fund social investment. Which ONE of the following best explains why the example matters to his argument?

options.text: Stakeholder language establishes that no commercial calculation is involved.
A public statement has exactly the same effect as enforceable legislation.
Public pledges necessarily prevent political lobbying.
The contrast can reveal the limits of voluntary commitments when concrete proposals affect profits.
Any opposition to one tax proposal proves that the company has no stakeholders.

questions.explanation: The historical example contrasts stakeholder rhetoric with lobbying on measures that affect companies’ financial interests. It supports Reich’s structural critique of voluntary CSR.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 7 — Why Corporate Social Responsibility is BS; assigned week(s): 5, 6

questions.stem: With reference to Reich’s argument, a company supports public infrastructure that also improves its own business prospects. Which ONE of the following would be an INCORRECT conclusion?

options.text: The example need not demonstrate that voluntary promises can replace public rules.
Corporate support can coincide with a commercial interest in the proposal.
The proposal may still have public benefits.
The company’s incentives are relevant to interpreting its position.
Support alone establishes that the company will sacrifice profits whenever a social need arises.

questions.explanation: Support for a mutually beneficial measure does not establish willingness to bear costs in every conflict between profit and social welfare.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 7 — Why Corporate Social Responsibility is BS; assigned week(s): 5, 6

chapters.title: Week 6 — Stakeholder Theory / CSR
chapters.description: Reading allocation follows the module outline; lecture questions retain delivered-week placement. Five options; single answer; AI-written practice.

questions.stem: In terms of stakeholder theory, which ONE of the following statements about shareholders and stakeholders is TRUE?

options.text: Stakeholders include only people with written contracts with the business.
Shareholders cease to be stakeholders when a firm adopts a stakeholder approach.
The terms are interchangeable because only share ownership creates a business interest.
Shareholders are one stakeholder group, but stakeholders also include other groups that affect or are affected by the business.
Stakeholders include only groups that can impose a financial loss on the business.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders include groups that affect or are affected by a business; shareholders are one such group, not the entire category.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 6 — original recording/transcript; Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82)

questions.stem: In the stakeholder classification in the assigned OpenStax reading, legislatures, regulators and boards are examples of which ONE of the following?

options.text: Functional output stakeholders.
Enabling stakeholders.
Functional input stakeholders.
Diffused stakeholders.
Normative stakeholders.

questions.explanation: In the assigned textbook’s classification, enabling stakeholders include regulators, legislatures and boards because of their authority or ability to enable operations.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82) — Textbook pp. 75–76.

questions.stem: In the stakeholder classification in the assigned OpenStax reading, competitors and industry peers that influence shared standards are examples of which ONE of the following?

options.text: Enabling stakeholders.
Functional input stakeholders.
Functional output stakeholders.
Normative stakeholders.
Diffused stakeholders.

questions.explanation: The textbook uses normative stakeholders for peers and competitors influencing shared norms. This category is distinct from the normative approach to stakeholder ethics.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82) — Textbook pp. 75–76; this category is distinct from the normative approach to stakeholder management.

questions.stem: With reference to the functional stakeholder category in the assigned OpenStax reading, which ONE of the following correctly pairs input stakeholders with output stakeholders?

options.text: Inputs: voters and community campaigners; outputs: regulators and boards.
Inputs: employees and suppliers; outputs: customers and distributors.
Inputs: customers and retailers; outputs: employees and suppliers.
Inputs: regulators and legislatures; outputs: boards and shareholders.
Inputs: news media and NGOs; outputs: competitors and industry peers.

questions.explanation: Employees and suppliers contribute inputs; customers and distributors are connected with outputs. These are two sides of the functional category.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82) — Textbook pp. 75–76.

questions.stem: In the stakeholder classification in the assigned OpenStax reading, which ONE of the following groups best fits the category of diffused stakeholders?

options.text: Regulators authorising the company’s operations.
Customers purchasing the company’s outputs.
Employees providing labour under contract.
Industry peers influencing shared professional norms.
NGOs and news media with an indirect connection to the company.

questions.explanation: Diffused stakeholders have indirect relationships, such as media or NGOs, rather than supplying inputs, buying outputs or exercising formal enabling authority.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82)

questions.stem: A company considers complaints from a community group only after managers conclude that a campaign could threaten profits. If the group could not affect business outcomes, managers would ignore it. In terms of stakeholder theory, which ONE of the following approaches is most clearly illustrated?

options.text: Virtue-based: the decision is explained solely by the managers’ cultivated character.
Descriptive: the company merely records stakeholder relationships without using them in decisions.
Kantian: managers disregard every consequence when deciding whom to consult.
Instrumental: stakeholder attention is linked to its expected effect on business outcomes.
Normative: residents’ interests are recognised as intrinsically important regardless of profit.

questions.explanation: An instrumental approach responds to stakeholders through expected business consequences. The scenario makes profit impact the condition for attention.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 6 — original recording/transcript; Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82)

questions.stem: A company takes a small group’s legitimate concern seriously even though the group has little influence and cannot cause a financial loss. Managers explain that those affected deserve fair consideration in their own right. In terms of stakeholder theory, this is an example of which ONE of the following?

options.text: A shareholder-only allocation model.
The instrumental stakeholder approach.
A purely descriptive stakeholder model.
The normative stakeholder approach.
Short-term ethical egoism.

questions.explanation: The normative approach recognises stakeholders’ intrinsic claims, rather than treating attention only as a means to commercial gain.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 6 — original recording/transcript; Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82)

questions.stem: With reference to the account of Irish corporate governance in the supplied lecture deck, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.text: Corporate governance consists only of informal preferences expressed by the board.
Governance codes and Acts of the Oireachtas always have identical binding force.
A shareholder agreement replaces every statutory duty applying to the company.
Company law, regulation, largely non-binding codes, constitutions and shareholder agreements can all contribute.
Only stock-exchange rules can impose governance requirements on Irish companies.

questions.explanation: The supplied governance account draws on several sources with different legal force. Non-binding codes are not identical to Acts.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides — Slide 1; a course-source question, not current legal advice.

questions.stem: According to the supplied material on protected disclosures, which ONE of the following most accurately describes the combination of conditions involved in recognising a protected disclosure?

options.text: Any personal disagreement reported publicly, regardless of its work context or content.
A complaint that qualifies solely because the employer disputes it.
Any statement made anonymously, regardless of reasonable belief or reporting conditions.
Information reasonably believed to show relevant wrongdoing, acquired in a work-related context and disclosed through the specified manner.
An allegation that is protected only after the worker obtains a criminal conviction.

questions.explanation: The deck combines reasonable belief, relevant wrongdoing, a work-related context and specified reporting conditions; none of these is replaced simply by publicity or anonymity.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides — Slides 5 and 9.

questions.stem: With reference to the distinction between protected disclosures and personal grievances in the supplied deck, which ONE of the following would generally be directed to an internal grievance procedure on the facts given?

options.text: Information reasonably believed to show a criminal offence in a work-related context.
An interpersonal conflict between a worker and another colleague.
A reasonably believed risk to the health and safety of workers.
Information suggesting the concealment of evidence of relevant wrongdoing.
Information about damage to the environment acquired through work.

questions.explanation: The deck generally distinguishes interpersonal grievances from reports of relevant wrongdoing. A personal conflict alone does not establish a protected disclosure.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides — Slide 5; the wording is “generally”, not an absolute exclusion of every possible workplace dispute.

questions.stem: A worker acquires information through work that gives reasonable grounds to believe a serious health or safety problem is likely to occur in the future. The worker has not yet suffered an injury. With reference to the supplied protected-disclosures material, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.text: Only past wrongdoing can be reported through the protected-disclosure framework.
Health and safety risks qualify only when environmental damage has already occurred.
Likely future wrongdoing can fall within the listed categories; a completed injury is not always required.
A report can qualify only if the worker has personally suffered the predicted injury.
The reporting route becomes irrelevant whenever a future risk is serious.

questions.explanation: The deck includes likely future wrongdoing among the matters that may be reported; it does not always require completed injury.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides — Slide 5.

questions.stem: According to the supplied protected-disclosures material, which option gives the COMPLETE set of groups covered by the list below, subject to the other reporting conditions?

options.text: Former employees and agency workers.
Trainees and volunteers.
Board members and shareholders.
a) and b) above.
a), b) and c) above.

questions.explanation: All three sets of groups appear in the deck’s list. Being within a listed group does not remove the other conditions for a protected disclosure.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides — Slide 9; reporting conditions still matter.

questions.stem: A worker considers reporting relevant wrongdoing to an external prescribed person rather than simply publishing the information. According to the supplied deck, which ONE of the following must be checked when choosing that recipient?

options.text: Every prescribed person has the same remit for every form of wrongdoing.
The recipient’s official title alone determines protection, regardless of the subject reported.
The wrongdoing should fall within the remit of the prescribed person selected.
An external report is necessarily the same as publishing the information on social media.
Using an external channel removes the need for reasonable belief.

questions.explanation: A prescribed person’s remit must match the wrongdoing reported. External reporting is not a route with identical coverage for every recipient.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides — Slides 10–11.

questions.stem: With reference to the deck’s discussion of protected disclosures and penalisation, which ONE of the following statements correctly distinguishes being covered from the route for obtaining redress?

options.text: Every covered group must bring a penalisation complaint through the same WRC route.
Anyone unable to use this WRC route is necessarily excluded from all protected-disclosure protection.
A report becomes protected only after the worker successfully obtains compensation.
An employer’s denial automatically settles whether penalisation followed a disclosure.
Board members and shareholders may seek civil-court redress rather than using this WRC complaint route.

questions.explanation: The deck distinguishes covered groups from the forum for redress: it identifies civil-court rather than this WRC complaint route for board members and shareholders.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides — Slides 11–12; no detailed remedy or time limit is inferred.

questions.stem: With reference to the Workplace Relations Commission as described in the supplied deck, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.text: It performs the principal leadership role of individual company boards.
It acts only as an appeal body for Labour Court determinations.
It deals only with criminal prosecutions of workplace misconduct.
Its functions include compliance, information, inspection and dispute-resolution services.
It is limited to issuing non-binding advice without any other workplace role.

questions.explanation: The WRC’s role includes information, compliance, inspection and dispute-resolution functions; it is not limited to appeals or criminal prosecution.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides — Slides 2–4.

questions.stem: With reference to the Labour Court processes described in the supplied deck, which ONE of the following distinctions is correct?

options.text: The Labour Court’s principal role is to carry out company inspections on behalf of boards.
An employment-rights appeal permits unrelated new claims to be added to the original case.
Industrial-relations recommendations are non-binding, whereas employment-rights determinations are legally binding.
Every recommendation and determination has the same non-binding status.
Every workplace complaint must begin in the Labour Court rather than the WRC.

questions.explanation: The deck distinguishes non-binding industrial-relations recommendations from binding employment-rights determinations.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides — Slides 6–8.

questions.stem: According to the stakeholder power–interest matrix discussed in the assigned OpenStax material, which ONE of the following statements is FALSE?

options.text: High-power, low-interest stakeholders should generally be kept satisfied.
Low-power, high-interest stakeholders should generally be kept informed.
A low-power group has no morally relevant interests and can therefore be excluded from ethical consideration.
A practical map of influence does not by itself determine whose interests have intrinsic value.
High-power, high-interest stakeholders usually require close management.

questions.explanation: A power–interest map helps plan engagement. Low power is not proof that a group lacks ethical standing or legitimate interests.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82)

questions.stem: According to the company-type qualifications in the supplied governance deck, which ONE of the following statements is FALSE?

options.text: Every Irish company may have one director, and that same person may always serve as the sole company secretary.
A body corporate cannot itself serve as a director in the account given.
The cited account requires at least two directors for a public company.
A private company limited by shares may have one director with a separate secretary.
The cited account distinguishes public companies from private companies limited by shares.

questions.explanation: The deck qualifies the single-director provision by company type and requires a separate secretary; it is not an unrestricted rule for every company.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides

questions.stem: With reference to the supplied deck’s description of larger company boards, which ONE of the following statements preserves the qualification in the source?

options.text: A company’s informal board preference replaces the applicable company law.
Larger companies generally combine executive and non-executive directors; “generally” should not be turned into an absolute rule about every company.
Non-executive directors are the same thing as incorporated bodies acting as directors.
A board must consist solely of executives because only employees may participate in governance.
Every private company is prohibited from appointing a non-executive director.

questions.explanation: The source describes a general pattern, not an absolute requirement applying identically to every company.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides

questions.stem: With reference to the core reading on warning labels for everyday food, which option gives the COMPLETE set of campaigners’ proposals below?

options.text: Warning labels on food products.
Salt-related taxes.
Restrictions on junk-food marketing or sports sponsorship.
a) and b) above.
a), b) and c) above.

questions.explanation: The reading reports all three as campaign proposals. Reporting a proposal is not the same as saying it has become law.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 8 — Warning labels on everyday food — These are reported proposals, not a claim that all were enacted.

questions.stem: According to the warning-label reading, which ONE of the following best distinguishes the case for mandatory reformulation from reliance on voluntary industry action?

options.text: The existence of a proposal establishes that it has already become law.
Industry investment proves that public-health targets have already been met.
Mandatory reformulation necessarily removes every role for consumers.
Mandatory rules can establish common requirements rather than depending on each firm choosing to change.
A voluntary promise has exactly the same enforceability as legislation.

questions.explanation: The article reports campaigners’ concern about the limits of voluntary action and their case for common enforceable requirements; proposals must not be mistaken for enacted law.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 8 — Warning labels on everyday food; assigned week(s): 6

questions.stem: With reference to the food-policy reading’s discussion of junk-food sponsorship of sport, which ONE of the following is the relevant concern?

options.text: A sponsorship agreement establishes that a product has independent medical approval.
Sponsorship can increase brand exposure and associate products with positive sporting experiences.
Sporting participation makes nutritional composition irrelevant.
Every spectator is proved to buy a sponsor’s product after each event.
Marketing restrictions mean that physical exercise has no public-health benefit.

questions.explanation: The reported concern is about promotional exposure and associations created by sponsorship, not proof of an identical effect on every spectator.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 8 — Warning labels on everyday food; assigned week(s): 6

questions.stem: The warning-label article reports an estimate of deaths that might be avoided by reducing salt consumption. Which ONE of the following is the correct way to interpret such a figure?

options.text: As proof that salt is the only cause of cardiovascular illness.
As an official count of future deaths that cannot vary with behaviour.
As a count of deaths already observed to have been prevented by the proposed policy.
As evidence that every reformulation proposal is already fully implemented.
As a conditional estimate dependent on the assumed reduction and the analysis behind it.

questions.explanation: An estimate of avoidable deaths describes a modelled or conditional potential effect, not an observed outcome of measures not yet implemented.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 8 — Warning labels on everyday food; assigned week(s): 6

questions.stem: According to the OpenStax reading’s classification of publics, a group that recognises a problem affecting it but has not yet organised to take action is best described as which ONE of the following?

options.text: An active public.
An aware public.
A latent public.
An enabling stakeholder by definition.
A nonpublic.

questions.explanation: An aware public recognises a problem but has not yet organised action. A latent public does not recognise it; an active public has begun to organise.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82)

questions.stem: According to the OpenStax classification of publics, a group is affected by a problem but has not yet recognised it. Which ONE of the following classifications is the closest fit?

options.text: A latent public.
A group with no stakeholder interest because it is unaware.
An active public.
An aware public.
An enabling institution solely because it is affected.

questions.explanation: A latent public is affected but has not recognised the problem. Awareness and organised action are distinct stages in the reading’s classification.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82); assigned week(s): 6

questions.stem: A researcher records which stakeholder groups a company consults and how it currently treats them, without yet judging whether the treatment is right or increases profits. According to Reading 9, which ONE of the following approaches is illustrated?

options.text: An exclusively normative assessment.
An instrumental claim that consultation must increase profit.
A finding that only shareholders qualify as stakeholders.
A calculation of a legally required minimum return.
A descriptive account of stakeholder relationships.

questions.explanation: A descriptive approach examines actual relationships and behaviour. Normative and instrumental approaches ask different questions about justification and outcomes.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82); assigned week(s): 6

questions.stem: A group that was aware of a company-related problem forms an association, coordinates complaints and begins a campaign. With reference to Reading 9’s classification of publics, which ONE of the following changes has occurred?

options.text: The group has ceased to be affected because it has organised.
The group has moved from awareness towards an active public.
The group has become latent because it now shares information.
The group’s claims have become morally conclusive solely through campaigning.
The group has necessarily acquired statutory regulatory powers.

questions.explanation: Organised action distinguishes an active public from one that is aware but has not mobilised. Activity does not by itself establish that every claim is correct.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82); assigned week(s): 6

chapters.title: Week 7 — Consumerism
chapters.description: Reading allocation follows the module outline; lecture questions retain delivered-week placement. Five options; single answer; AI-written practice.

questions.stem: According to Carroll’s CSR pyramid, discussed in class, which ONE of the following gives the responsibilities in the correct order from the base upwards?

options.text: Philanthropic, ethical, legal, economic.
Economic, legal, ethical, philanthropic.
Legal, economic, philanthropic, ethical.
Economic, philanthropic, legal, ethical.
Ethical, legal, economic, philanthropic.

questions.explanation: Carroll’s pyramid places economic responsibilities at the base, followed by legal, ethical and philanthropic responsibilities.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: With reference to the commercial arguments for responsible corporate conduct, which option gives the COMPLETE set of possible benefits below?

options.text: Retaining customers and employees over the longer term.
Maintaining community support and a social licence to operate.
Managing risk and uncertainty affecting the business.
a) and b) above.
a), b) and c) above.

questions.explanation: Retention, a social licence to operate and risk management are all commercial arguments for responsible conduct; they explain potential business benefits rather than proving a duty-based motive.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: Which ONE of the following is principally a moral argument for corporate responsibility, rather than a claim that responsible conduct will improve business performance?

options.text: Responsible conduct can help retain commercially valuable customers.
A positive reputation can make recruiting skilled employees easier.
A company should address harms for which it bears responsibility even where doing so offers no competitive advantage.
Lower material waste can reduce a company’s production costs.
Community approval can reduce obstacles to a company’s operations.

questions.explanation: The moral argument concerns responsibility for harm even without a competitive payoff. The other options describe commercial benefits.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: An employer offers accommodation that improves workers’ living conditions. However, workers who leave or challenge the employer may risk losing both their income and their home. With reference to the lecture’s discussion of corporate benefits and dependency, which ONE of the following interpretations is most appropriate?

options.text: The housing arrangement has no ethical relevance because it lies outside wages.
The existence of a benefit establishes that the employment relationship is ethically satisfactory.
A benefit can improve living conditions while also creating dependency and unequal power.
An employee’s initial acceptance removes every later concern about bargaining power.
The possibility of dependency proves that all employer-provided benefits should be abolished.

questions.explanation: Employer-provided housing can provide a real benefit and also increase dependency, especially where challenging management threatens both income and shelter.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: With reference to the discussion of B Corp and independent certification, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.text: Independent assessment differs from a company merely making its own claims, but does not remove the need to scrutinise particular conduct.
Certification means that the company cannot pursue a commercial return.
A certified company no longer needs to disclose its supply-chain practices.
A company’s own description of its values is identical to independent certification.
Certification establishes that every product and business decision is ethically beyond criticism.

questions.explanation: Independent certification differs from self-assertion, but it does not establish ethical perfection or remove scrutiny of particular products and practices.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: A company advertises its support for a social cause while evidence about its supply chain appears inconsistent with the advertised commitment. Which ONE of the following questions should be given priority in evaluating whether the campaign is substantive rather than purpose-washing?

options.text: Whether any social-purpose message must be rejected regardless of what the firm actually does.
Whether the campaign is popular enough to make operational evidence unnecessary.
Whether the campaign’s production budget establishes the sincerity of the commitment.
Whether the public commitment is supported by substantive changes in corporate conduct.
Whether publicity alone is an adequate substitute for examining affected workers’ circumstances.

questions.explanation: A social-purpose message should be checked against substantive operations. Publicity, popularity and expenditure alone do not establish responsible conduct.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript; Reading 3 — Woke-washing and culture-war branding

questions.stem: With reference to the lecture and Pretty et al.’s reading on wellbeing, which ONE of the following best explains why GDP growth alone is an incomplete measure of improvement in people’s lives?

options.text: It directly measures the distribution of every improvement in health and social connection.
It records only non-market activities such as unpaid care.
It does not by itself capture health, relationships, environmental conditions and the quality of everyday life.
A rise in output establishes that all six wellbeing pathways have improved.
An unchanged GDP figure establishes that nobody’s wellbeing can improve.

questions.explanation: GDP does not by itself measure the health, relationships and environmental conditions central to the wellbeing discussion.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript; Reading 10 — Improving wellbeing independently of GDP

questions.stem: With reference to the critique of consumerism in the module, which ONE of the following statements gives the most balanced account of its possible benefits and costs?

options.text: Every increase in consumption necessarily produces an equal increase in subjective wellbeing.
Consumer choice proves that marketing cannot influence the pattern of demand.
The existence of material comfort removes the possibility of harmful consumption.
Criticism of consumerism requires denying that any purchased good can improve life.
Consumption may provide convenience and choice while also contributing to waste and status-driven dissatisfaction.

questions.explanation: A balanced account recognises both the conveniences of consumption and its possible social and environmental costs, rather than treating either side as exhaustive.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript; Reading 11 — Marketing, consumer society and hedonism

questions.stem: According to the supplied protected-disclosures material, which option gives the COMPLETE set of possible relevant-wrongdoing categories below?

options.text: A criminal offence reported in the required work-related context.
A health or safety risk falling within the listed categories.
Concealment or destruction of evidence relating to relevant wrongdoing.
a) and b) above.
a), b) and c) above.

questions.explanation: The deck lists all three categories. Relevant belief, work-context and reporting conditions still matter.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides

questions.stem: With reference to a claim of penalisation following a protected disclosure, which ONE of the following statements reflects the supplied deck?

options.text: Every worker must obtain a criminal conviction before the issue of penalisation can be considered.
An employer’s denial alone establishes that the action was unrelated to the disclosure.
The employer must show that the act or omission was justified on other grounds, rather than relying solely on an unsupported denial.
Being covered means that every group must use exactly the same redress forum.
An employer may treat the making of any disclosure as automatic justification for a penalty.

questions.explanation: The deck identifies an employer burden to justify the action on other grounds. This is distinct from deciding which forum is available to a particular group.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides

questions.stem: In terms of Carroll’s CSR pyramid, which ONE of the following is NOT one of its four named responsibilities?

options.text: Legal responsibilities.
Competitive responsibilities.
Ethical responsibilities.
Philanthropic responsibilities.
Economic responsibilities.

questions.explanation: The four named layers are economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic. Competitive performance is not a separately named layer.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: A company argues that because it donates to local charities, it need not examine serious harm arising from its ordinary operations. With reference to the module’s critique of corporate responsibility, which ONE of the following is the strongest response?

options.text: Philanthropy does not by itself settle whether the core operations meet their ethical responsibilities.
Community approval removes the need to examine the affected workers’ circumstances.
Any donation establishes that the company’s overall conduct is ethical.
A profitable donation is automatically incapable of producing any benefit.
Ethical responsibility applies to charitable activity but not to the company’s business model.

questions.explanation: A favourable charitable action and the ethical acceptability of a firm’s core practices are separate matters; one is not an automatic offset for the other.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript; Reading 7 — Why Corporate Social Responsibility is BS

questions.stem: According to Pretty et al.’s discussion of sustainable behaviour, why might adding greener purchases while leaving all other consumption unchanged fall short of the proposal?

options.text: The paper says that any purchased object is incapable of contributing to wellbeing.
The paper emphasises substituting sustainable activities and patterns for resource-intensive consumption, not simply adding another layer of purchases.
The paper argues that non-material activities have no role in wellbeing.
The paper measures sustainability only by the number of environmental labels purchased.
An additional green product necessarily cancels the effects of every other purchase.

questions.explanation: Substitution matters: adding a green purchase does not necessarily reduce the impacts of unchanged consumption elsewhere.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 10 — Improving wellbeing independently of GDP

questions.stem: With reference to Pretty et al.’s assessment of consumption externalities and positive countertrends, which ONE of the following is TRUE?

options.text: The existence of positive countertrends does not mean the paper concludes that every wellbeing factor has a positive overall balance.
Mixed evidence means that the authors cannot identify a substantial deficit for any factor.
The scorecard concerns GDP alone and excludes health, community and nature.
Identifying a positive countertrend establishes that the corresponding negative externalities no longer exist.
The paper concludes that every factor has an unambiguously positive balance.

questions.explanation: The paper’s scorecard is mixed, with most factors in substantial deficit. Positive developments are reported alongside continuing costs, not as proof that every balance is positive.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 10 — Improving wellbeing independently of GDP

questions.stem: According to Pretty et al.’s discussion of possessions and wellbeing, which ONE of the following best illustrates “cathexis”?

options.text: Increasing consumption primarily to maintain rank relative to other consumers.
Measuring an object’s value solely by its resale price.
Assuming that buying a greener product cancels every impact of additional consumption.
Replacing a serviceable object whenever a newer model becomes available.
Valuing and caring for an object because of the emotional meaning attached to it.

questions.explanation: Cathexis is emotional investment in a possession. It can make an object meaningful and worth caring for rather than replacing simply for novelty.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 10 — Improving wellbeing independently of GDP

questions.stem: According to Pretty et al., which ONE of the following best illustrates social capital as a contributor to wellbeing?

options.text: A rise in consumption regardless of changes in social relationships.
The amount of national output divided by population.
The number of advertisements viewed during a working day.
Relationships of trust, reciprocity and support within a community.
The resale value of a household’s newest possessions.

questions.explanation: Pretty et al. discuss social capital through networks, relationships, trust and reciprocity rather than equating it with material wealth or national output.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 10 — Improving wellbeing independently of GDP; assigned week(s): 7

questions.stem: A community walking group offers physical activity, contact with nature and regular social interaction. With reference to Pretty et al., which ONE of the following is TRUE?

options.text: It can contribute to several wellbeing pathways at once without requiring an equivalent rise in purchased goods.
Its effects can be assessed only by the value of shoes purchased by participants.
An activity can contribute to only one of the six pathways at a time.
Its benefits must be excluded unless participants pay a commercial membership fee.
Contact with nature prevents the activity from having a social benefit.

questions.explanation: The pathways can reinforce one another. An activity can support an active body, natural connections and community relationships without being defined by expenditure.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 10 — Improving wellbeing independently of GDP; assigned week(s): 7

questions.stem: With reference to Pretty et al.’s argument about health and wellbeing, which ONE of the following would be an INCORRECT policy inference?

options.text: Changes in food, activity and social connections may affect wellbeing.
An increase in expenditure on illness necessarily demonstrates an equivalent improvement in underlying wellbeing.
Measures beyond GDP can help distinguish costs from improvements in quality of life.
Rising expenditure on treating illness can coexist with avoidable burdens.
Preventive improvements to everyday life can matter alongside clinical treatment.

questions.explanation: Expenditure associated with illness is not automatically a net improvement in wellbeing. The reading examines prevention and pathways beyond GDP alone.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 10 — Improving wellbeing independently of GDP; assigned week(s): 7

questions.stem: According to O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, in the core reading on marketing, consumer society and hedonism, which ONE of the following best represents their conclusion about marketing’s role in consumerism?

options.text: Marketing created materialism from nothing in societies that previously had no such desires.
The costs of consumer society establish that it provides no convenience or freedom of choice.
Marketing has acted more as a facilitator than as the sole manufacturer of consumerism.
Consumers passively accept marketing messages without interpretation or resistance.
The authors conclude that marketing has no influence on consumption patterns.

questions.explanation: The authors conclude that marketing has been more facilitator than manufacturer of consumerism; they do not describe consumers as wholly passive or deny marketing any influence.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 11 — Marketing, consumer society and hedonism — Conclusion, article p. 544 / PDF p. 21.

questions.stem: According to O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, what is a limitation of the “hypodermic” or simple stimulus–response view of marketing’s influence?

options.text: It requires every advertisement to contain the same literal message.
It assumes that consumers cannot ever encounter advertising.
It assumes that marketing consists only of legally prohibited statements.
It gives insufficient attention to consumers’ interpretation, negotiation and resistance.
It treats consumers as the sole authors of every product on sale.

questions.explanation: The article contrasts a passive or reactive consumer model with negotiated meaning and co-production; consumers are not simply injected with fixed responses.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 11 — Marketing, consumer society and hedonism; assigned week(s): 7

questions.stem: With reference to the marketing and hedonism reading, which ONE of the following best illustrates “psychological obsolescence”?

options.text: A manufacturer has exhausted the raw material needed for repair.
A retailer reduces stock because the product has reached its physical expiry date.
A consumer replaces a serviceable product because newer models make it seem out of date.
A legal authority prohibits a product from being sold.
A product can no longer operate because an essential component has failed.

questions.explanation: Psychological obsolescence concerns the perceived datedness of a functioning product, encouraging replacement despite continued serviceability.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 11 — Marketing, consumer society and hedonism; assigned week(s): 7

questions.stem: According to the balanced discussion of consumer society in the marketing and hedonism article, which ONE of the following is TRUE?

options.text: Marketing’s influence establishes that consumers have no interpretive agency.
Any criticism of materialism proves that marketing created every material desire.
Acknowledging choice and convenience requires denying that waste occurs.
Consumer society can offer benefits while also generating waste and dissatisfaction associated with excessive material concerns.
The authors conclude that every increase in consumption must increase subjective wellbeing.

questions.explanation: The authors acknowledge benefits such as choice and convenience as well as waste and the limits of material consumption as a route to wellbeing.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 11 — Marketing, consumer society and hedonism; assigned week(s): 7

questions.stem: With reference to the core critique of TOMS Shoes, which ONE of the following distinctions is central when assessing a purchase-linked donation?

options.text: The number of shoes delivered by itself measures every relevant educational and welfare outcome.
An in-kind donation necessarily produces no benefit for any recipient.
A donor’s positive feeling and good intention do not establish that the intervention best addresses recipients’ needs.
A purchase-linked donation proves that structural poverty has been removed.
Recipients’ own circumstances are irrelevant once a donation is free.

questions.explanation: The TOMS critique distinguishes donor satisfaction and outputs from evidence of benefit in recipients’ circumstances. Good intentions do not settle effectiveness.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 12 — Critique of TOMS Shoes

questions.stem: With reference to the TOMS reading and its discussion of evidence, why is finding that recipients use donated shoes not sufficient to establish the programme’s broader success?

options.text: Use of a donated item proves that recipients’ needs were assessed optimally.
Use establishes that a cash alternative would have exactly the same effect.
Use cannot by itself establish wider effects such as improved attendance, health or wellbeing.
Use demonstrates that a donation has no value of any kind.
Use removes the need to consider the costs of providing the donation.

questions.explanation: Receipt and use are different outcomes from the broader benefits claimed for an intervention. The reading discusses evidence rather than treating intentions or use as sufficient.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 12 — Critique of TOMS Shoes; assigned week(s): 7

questions.stem: The critique of TOMS asks whether cash or another form of support might better meet recipients’ needs. Which ONE of the following is the strongest interpretation of that comparison?

options.text: Cash must always be the best intervention in every setting.
Alternative interventions should be compared using recipients’ needs and evidence, not donor satisfaction alone.
In-kind support is necessarily worthless regardless of context.
A popular retail model establishes that no alternative should be tested.
Recipients cannot have relevant knowledge about their own priorities.

questions.explanation: The comparison invites examination of opportunity cost and recipients’ priorities. It does not justify a universal claim that cash or in-kind aid is always superior.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 12 — Critique of TOMS Shoes; assigned week(s): 7

questions.stem: With reference to the appended discussion of research on shoe donations in Reading 12, which ONE of the following best distinguishes evidence from an exaggerated claim?

options.text: A small negative local-market effect is not the same as proof that donations destroy the entire local industry.
The research establishes an identical effect for every type of donation in every country.
A retail brand’s good intentions settle the size of any local-market effect.
Any negative effect establishes that recipients never use donated shoes.
The absence of catastrophic damage proves that donations maximise recipients’ welfare.

questions.explanation: The appended evidence describes limited effects rather than the sweeping claim of total market destruction. Neither overstatement nor a claim of universally optimal aid follows.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 12 — Critique of TOMS Shoes; assigned week(s): 7

chapters.title: Week 8 — Fortune at the Bottom of the Pyramid
chapters.description: Reading allocation follows the module outline; lecture questions retain delivered-week placement. Five options; single answer; AI-written practice.

questions.stem: With reference to the discussion of degrowth in Lecture 8, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.text: A requirement that low-income households give up access to basic goods.
A policy limited to reducing all household purchases by the same percentage.
A temporary fall in GDP with no change to institutions or social priorities.
A broader reorganisation of social priorities and ways of living, rather than simply asking everyone to buy less.
A strategy for increasing consumption indefinitely by changing product labels.

questions.explanation: The lecture presents degrowth as a broader change in priorities and social organisation, not merely an equal cut in every person’s purchases or an unplanned recession.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: According to the broader account of degrowth discussed in class, which option gives the COMPLETE set of compatible practices below?

options.text: Sharing resources and supporting commons.
Recognising care and other non-market activity.
Seeking higher relative status through continually increasing material consumption.
a) and b) above.
a), b) and c) above.

questions.explanation: Sharing, commons and care fit the broader degrowth discussion; escalating material consumption to pursue status does not.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: A student argues that any proposal to reduce affluent consumption must also require people in severe poverty to give up access to basic goods. With reference to the lecture’s distinction between excess consumption and unmet needs, which ONE of the following is the best response?

options.text: The existence of poverty establishes that total consumption can grow without environmental constraints.
Every purchase by a low-income household is necessarily a basic need.
Affluent consumers have no responsibility for resource use because markets reflect demand.
The same proportional reduction in consumption has identical consequences at every income level.
Reducing excess in affluent settings need not imply denying essential goods and opportunities to low-income groups.

questions.explanation: The lecture distinguishes reducing affluent excess from meeting unmet needs. An identical consumption cut can have very different effects at different income levels.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: Households increase spending on visible goods in an effort to improve their status relative to one another. If all households do this, which ONE of the following is a relevant limitation of the strategy?

options.text: The resulting demand has no connection to resource consumption.
Every household must move upward in the status ranking by the same amount.
Relative position necessarily improves whenever absolute spending rises.
Material spending can increase without everyone improving their relative status.
A status comparison measures the same thing as the satisfaction of an unmet basic need.

questions.explanation: Relative status is comparative: everyone spending more does not mean everyone rises relative to everyone else.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: According to the pro-Bottom-of-the-Pyramid approach discussed in class, which ONE of the following best describes how a market serving low-income customers may be commercially viable?

options.text: Products should be designed for affluent markets and sold unchanged regardless of local conditions.
Low individual incomes mean that no commercially viable market can exist.
Large numbers of customers and suitable low-cost models can make low-margin transactions commercially attractive.
Commercial sales to poor customers establish poverty reduction without any further evidence.
Low margins eliminate the need to consider distribution and transaction costs.

questions.explanation: The pro-BOP model can combine small margins with large numbers of customers, but requires suitable cost and distribution models and does not itself prove development impact.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript; Reading 13 — Selling to the Poor

questions.stem: A company sells detergent in sachets that a low-income customer can afford today, although the price per gram is higher than for a large pack. Which ONE of the following statements about this example is TRUE?

options.text: The smallest pack necessarily offers the best value per gram.
A low purchase price eliminates the need to consider packaging waste.
Affordability today and long-run unit cost are the same measure.
A higher unit price establishes that access has not changed at all.
Lower upfront cost can improve access without producing the lowest unit price.

questions.explanation: A small package can be accessible within today’s budget while costing more per gram. Upfront affordability and unit value are different measures.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript; Reading 14 — The mirage of marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid

questions.stem: An appliance is redesigned to work where electricity and water supplies are unreliable. Its features respond to conditions that do not arise in the company’s usual affluent market. With reference to the BOP discussion, which ONE of the following principles is illustrated?

options.text: Design should respond to the conditions in which customers will actually use the product.
Lower-income customers necessarily prefer fewer useful functions regardless of context.
The availability of an appliance guarantees a particular household income increase.
A standard affluent-market product can always be transferred unchanged.
Customers’ local infrastructure is separate from the value of the product.

questions.explanation: Product design must fit actual infrastructure and use conditions. Adaptation can make a product useful without guaranteeing a particular income outcome.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: With reference to the mobile-money example in Lecture 8, which ONE of the following most accurately describes the contribution of the model to financial access?

options.text: Providing charitable grants that recipients never have to exchange or collect.
Requiring every sender and recipient to own a smartphone and a conventional bank account.
Using local agents and basic mobile-phone access to make money transfers available without relying on conventional bank access.
Replacing all cash handling with a system that has no local agents.
Eliminating all transaction costs merely by using a mobile network.

questions.explanation: The mobile-money example uses local agents and mobile access to enable transfers where conventional banking access is limited; it does not require smartphones for everyone.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: With reference to the discussion of recycling activity in Dharavi, which ONE of the following conclusions avoids both dismissing economic activity and romanticising poor conditions?

options.text: Recycling revenue removes the need to examine health and safety.
Poor living conditions establish that residents perform no economically valuable activity.
Informal enterprise and hazardous work cannot occur in the same place.
The existence of profitable recycling establishes that working conditions are satisfactory.
Economic value and entrepreneurial activity can coexist with hazardous work and poor living conditions.

questions.explanation: Economic activity and entrepreneurial effort can coexist with serious hazards. Neither romanticising poverty nor denying residents’ economic contribution is justified.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: With reference to the debate between a consumer-market BOP argument and Karnani’s critique, which ONE of the following comparisons is TRUE?

options.text: The debate concerns advertising style only, rather than income, production or welfare.
Karnani treats every low-price consumer product as sufficient evidence of poverty reduction.
Karnani emphasises poor people’s role as producers and the need to raise real incomes, rather than treating sales alone as poverty reduction.
The pro-BOP argument requires that poor people be excluded from markets.
Karnani argues that the private sector can have no role in improving poor people’s lives.

questions.explanation: Karnani’s critique shifts attention to production and real income. Selling goods profitably and reducing poverty are different claims.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript; Reading 13 — Selling to the Poor; Reading 14 — The mirage of marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid

questions.stem: A business asks low-income customers to help identify how a product will be used, what infrastructure is available and which features matter most. With reference to BOP approaches, which ONE of the following best explains the value of this participation?

options.text: It can improve the fit between the offer and users’ actual circumstances instead of assuming that an affluent-market design will transfer unchanged.
It establishes that all low-income customers have identical needs.
It removes the need to examine price, distribution or financing terms.
It replaces the need to consider whether a useful product is affordable.
It proves that every product the business subsequently sells will reduce poverty.

questions.explanation: Participation can improve design and relevance, but does not by itself guarantee affordability, welfare or poverty reduction.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript; Reading 13 — Selling to the Poor

questions.stem: With reference to small sachets in BOP markets, which ONE of the following statements is FALSE?

options.text: Packaging waste can remain relevant when evaluating the model.
A small sachet may make a product accessible within a limited daily budget.
Accessibility and long-term value are different considerations.
A lower cash price for one sachet necessarily means a lower price per unit and a lower environmental impact.
A customer can face a higher unit cost despite a lower upfront price.

questions.explanation: Small portions can improve immediate access while carrying higher unit costs or packaging burdens. Neither value nor impact follows from pack size alone.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript; Reading 14 — The mirage of marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid

questions.stem: According to Karnani’s critique of the BOP argument, which option gives the COMPLETE set of statements that accurately reflect his position?

options.text: Improving poor people’s productive opportunities and real incomes is important.
Profitable consumer sales and demonstrated poverty reduction are different outcomes.
Every profitable sale to a low-income customer is sufficient proof that development has occurred.
a) and b) above.
a), b) and c) above.

questions.explanation: Karnani stresses production and income and questions the inference from sales to poverty reduction. The third statement is the assumption being criticised, not an accepted criterion.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 14 — The mirage of marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid; Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript

questions.stem: According to Hammond and Prahalad’s pro-BOP argument, which ONE of the following potential contributions of business is illustrated by the e-Choupal example?

options.text: Guaranteeing that every commercial transaction with a poor person eliminates poverty.
Improving producers’ access to information and markets in ways that can combine economic opportunity with inclusion.
Excluding low-income groups from market participation until they become affluent.
Removing producers’ ability to compare prices so that transactions become faster.
Substituting product advertising for any change in information or distribution.

questions.explanation: The e-Choupal example concerns information and market access for producers, illustrating a possible commercial contribution to economic inclusion.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 13 — Selling to the Poor

questions.stem: In Hammond and Prahalad’s discussion of e-Choupal, which ONE of the following best explains the importance of farmers gaining access to market information?

options.text: It makes agricultural production unnecessary.
It can improve bargaining and choices by reducing dependence on others’ control of price information.
It converts all farmers into customers without affecting their role as producers.
It removes every need for transport and distribution.
It guarantees that farmers receive a fixed profit regardless of prices.

questions.explanation: The e-Choupal example links information access to farmers’ decisions and market participation. It does not establish that all other constraints or risks disappear.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 13 — Selling to the Poor; assigned week(s): 8

questions.stem: According to the pro-BOP reading, which ONE of the following would be LEAST consistent with developing a viable offering for low-income markets?

options.text: Exploring innovations that reduce costs while providing useful value.
Investigating the circumstances in which customers will obtain and use a product.
Assuming that an unchanged affluent-market product and distribution system will automatically fit local conditions.
Adapting distribution to reach people excluded from conventional channels.
Treating low-income customers as people with choices and aspirations.

questions.explanation: The pro-BOP approach calls for innovation and attention to excluded customers’ circumstances, rather than assuming an existing affluent-market model will transfer unchanged.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 13 — Selling to the Poor; assigned week(s): 8

questions.stem: With reference to Hammond and Prahalad’s argument, which ONE of the following best describes the relationship between business opportunity and poverty-related exclusion?

options.text: Commercial participation means that public institutions have no role in development.
A market opportunity can arise from reducing exclusion and improving access, rather than treating poor people solely as recipients of charity.
A sale establishes that poverty has been eliminated for the purchaser.
Poor people’s preferences become irrelevant once a product is inexpensive.
A business opportunity establishes that every customer will obtain a net welfare gain.

questions.explanation: The pro-BOP argument connects inclusion and opportunity, but the existence of a market does not itself prove universal welfare gains or eliminate other development responsibilities.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 13 — Selling to the Poor; assigned week(s): 8

questions.stem: According to Karnani’s critique of the Bottom of the Pyramid, which ONE of the following conclusions should NOT be accepted without further evidence about poverty reduction?

options.text: Growth in sales to poor consumers is, by itself, sufficient evidence that poverty has been reduced.
Poor people should be considered as producers as well as consumers.
Increasing poor people’s real income is important to poverty reduction.
A profitable opportunity and a development outcome are distinct claims requiring evidence.
The unit cost of small packages matters when assessing value.

questions.explanation: Karnani challenges treating consumer sales as sufficient evidence of poverty reduction; real income and productive opportunities must also be assessed.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 14 — The mirage of marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid

questions.stem: According to Karnani’s critique, why must estimates of BOP purchasing power in purchasing-power-parity terms be treated carefully when assessing a multinational’s potential market?

options.text: PPP and market exchange rates are interchangeable for all commercial purposes.
A large aggregate PPP figure eliminates distribution and affordability constraints.
The use of PPP means that poor people have no purchasing power at all.
A PPP estimate is not automatically revenue or profit that a firm can realise and repatriate at market exchange rates.
PPP estimates establish that every poor household can buy the same commercial product.

questions.explanation: Karnani distinguishes purchasing-power comparisons from a firm’s realisable commercial market, including the relevance of exchange rates and assumptions behind market estimates.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 14 — The mirage of marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid; assigned week(s): 8

questions.stem: A company sells an aspirational product in very small packs and reports strong demand from poor households. According to Karnani’s argument, which ONE of the following would still need to be established before claiming poverty alleviation?

options.text: That the company’s brand is visible in the community.
That the packs can be purchased individually.
That the company has a large advertising budget.
That the transaction improves poor people’s real welfare or income rather than merely increasing company sales.
That the company describes customers as empowered.

questions.explanation: Demand, affordability of a single pack and company revenue do not themselves demonstrate poverty reduction. Karnani asks for evidence of real benefit to poor people.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 14 — The mirage of marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid; assigned week(s): 8

questions.stem: With reference to Karnani’s critique of an undifferentiated “bottom of the pyramid” market, which ONE of the following is TRUE?

options.text: An aggregate market estimate can obscure differences in income, needs and the practical costs of reaching customers.
Market size alone guarantees a profitable distribution system.
All low-income households face identical conditions because they appear in the same income category.
A broad income category establishes that each household has the same disposable income.
The existence of any successful business case validates every market-size estimate.

questions.explanation: Karnani questions sweeping market claims. Aggregation can conceal purchasing constraints, heterogeneity and costs that affect both viability and welfare.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 14 — The mirage of marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid; assigned week(s): 8

chapters.title: Week 9 — Microfinance / Fairtrade
chapters.description: Outline-assigned reading coverage; this is not confirmation of lecture delivery. Five options; single answer; AI-written practice.

questions.stem: According to Rugasira’s critique of Fairtrade, which ONE of the following is most important beyond relying on compassionate consumer purchases and small premiums alone?

options.text: Replace all producer enterprise with dependence on charitable purchases.
Treat a consumer’s compassionate intention as sufficient evidence of development.
Assume that removing tariffs automatically removes every non-tariff barrier.
Enable producers to add value locally and obtain meaningful market access, rather than relying only on small premiums.
Concentrate all processing abroad because the location of value addition is irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Rugasira emphasises value addition and meaningful market access, rather than assuming that premiums alone provide durable development.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 15 — “Fairtrade is Not the Solution”
