questions.stem: According to Rugasira’s Fairtrade critique, why does the location of processing, roasting and packaging matter for coffee producers?

options.text: Consumers’ compassion removes the need to examine the structure of the value chain.
More value may be retained in producing economies when they can undertake higher-value stages of the chain.
Processing location has no effect on where economic value is retained.
Exporting unprocessed beans guarantees that producers capture the final retail value.
A certification premium necessarily transfers ownership of overseas brands to farmers.

questions.explanation: Rugasira emphasises value addition and market access beyond small premiums for primary commodities, including which economies capture processing and branding value.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 15 — “Fairtrade is Not the Solution”; assigned week(s): 9

questions.stem: With reference to Rugasira’s argument, which ONE of the following is FALSE?

options.text: The absence of a tariff establishes that producers have equal access to finance and retail markets.
Access to finance can constrain producers’ efforts to move into higher-value activity.
Market access can depend on barriers other than tariffs.
A compassionate purchase can coexist with structural limits on producers’ opportunities.
Removing a tariff does not automatically resolve every practical obstacle to selling higher-value products.

questions.explanation: The article discusses structural and non-tariff obstacles. Tariff removal does not establish that financing and market access have become equal.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 15 — “Fairtrade is Not the Solution”; assigned week(s): 9

questions.stem: A campaign encourages consumers to pay a small premium but gives no attention to producers’ access to capital or to higher-value markets. According to Rugasira, which ONE of the following is the strongest criticism?

options.text: A premium automatically gives producers the ability to finance processing facilities.
Any premium must leave every producer worse off.
Development is determined solely by the generosity of individual shoppers.
Consumers can have no useful role in trade-related change.
The campaign may leave the structural constraints on long-term development substantially unchanged.

questions.explanation: Rugasira’s critique is that compassionate consumption and premiums alone are not substitutes for finance, value addition and meaningful market access.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 15 — “Fairtrade is Not the Solution”; assigned week(s): 9

questions.stem: With reference to the Kiva reading, which ONE of the following statements correctly distinguishes the platform’s lender-facing description from the costs that borrowers may face?

options.text: Kiva not charging interest directly does not mean that partner microfinance institutions charge borrowers no interest.
The absence of a lender return establishes that the borrower faces no fees or financing cost.
A personal borrower story establishes the exact welfare effect of the loan.
A non-profit intermediary’s status prevents every partner from charging interest.
Every amount supplied through the platform is a gift rather than a repayable loan.

questions.explanation: Borrower cost depends on partner institutions’ terms as well as the platform’s own model. No direct interest charged by Kiva does not imply a free loan for the borrower.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 16 — Criticisms of Kiva

questions.stem: The Kiva reading contains strong claims by its critic and editorial notes reporting Kiva’s responses. Which ONE of the following is the most appropriate way to use that source?

options.text: Treat every allegation as independently established current fact.
Assume that an editorial response proves all allegations false.
Treat the age of the article as proof that present practices are identical.
Ignore the critic because a response was published.
Distinguish the author’s claims from disputed points and check the evidence behind each.

questions.explanation: The source includes competing claims and responses. Source-specific questions should preserve attribution and dispute rather than turning the article into a verified present-day verdict.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 16 — Criticisms of Kiva; assigned week(s): 9

questions.stem: According to Sinclair’s critique of Kiva, why is the individual borrower’s story not sufficient to evaluate the lending mechanism?

options.text: Intermediary institutions cannot charge borrowers if the website is non-profit.
A moving narrative proves that the loan caused a lasting increase in income.
Funds move through intermediary institutions whose costs, incentives and practices also require scrutiny.
The borrower’s photograph establishes the full terms of the loan.
The story establishes that lenders have directly negotiated the borrower’s contract.

questions.explanation: Sinclair focuses on intermediary MFIs and the difference between a lender-facing narrative and the financing arrangements. The explanation remains an account of his critique.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 16 — Criticisms of Kiva; assigned week(s): 9

questions.stem: With reference to the Kiva article’s discussion of portfolio yields and loan interest rates, which ONE of the following is the relevant transparency question?

options.text: Whether an institutional average must equal the terms of every individual loan.
Whether a borrower’s photograph is sufficiently memorable.
Whether non-profit status prevents any difference between headline figures and borrower costs.
Whether charitable language removes the need to disclose charges.
Whether the reported measure accurately communicates the actual cost faced by borrowers.

questions.explanation: The critic questions reliance on portfolio yields rather than actual loan rates, while the editorial note records Kiva’s response. The relevant issue is what the measure reveals about borrower costs.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 16 — Criticisms of Kiva; assigned week(s): 9

questions.stem: With reference to the core article on Nestlé and forced labour in the Thai seafood supply chain, which ONE of the following is the most defensible interpretation of a company’s disclosure of a problem?

options.text: Disclosure can be significant while still leaving questions about hidden risks and effective remediation.
Only final consumers have responsibilities for the disclosed conditions.
A disclosure in one supply chain resolves every controversy involving the company.
Admitting a problem proves that every supplier has already remedied it.
The existence of a disclosure establishes that no further independent scrutiny is needed.

questions.explanation: Disclosure can be important without establishing that every problem is solved. Risk identification and effective remediation remain separate questions.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 17 — Nestlé: corporate conduct and responsibility

questions.stem: The Nestlé article discusses Thai seafood supply chains and also refers to allegations involving cocoa in another country. Which ONE of the following is TRUE?

options.text: A corporate response in Thailand legally resolves litigation concerning cocoa.
Supply-chain problems can be related ethically while remaining distinct factual and legal cases.
The different products establish that the cases cannot raise any common ethical questions.
Disclosure of one case establishes that no other supply chain needs investigation.
A finding in one supply chain automatically establishes every allegation in the other.

questions.explanation: The article places separate contexts alongside one another. Their ethical relevance does not merge their facts or legal outcomes.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 17 — Nestlé: corporate conduct and responsibility; assigned week(s): 9

questions.stem: With reference to the Nestlé seafood article, why is the investigation by Verité relevant?

options.text: It establishes that finished-product quality determines all labour conditions.
It replaces the need for a company to take remedial action.
It certifies that every supplier worldwide is free from labour abuse.
It means that customers can infer conditions from the product’s packaging alone.
It provides scrutiny of labour conditions beyond relying solely on the company’s public assurances.

questions.explanation: The investigation supplies evidence about labour conditions and risks. It does not amount to a universal clean bill of health or a substitute for remediation.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 17 — Nestlé: corporate conduct and responsibility; assigned week(s): 9

questions.stem: According to the forced-labour supply-chain reading, which ONE of the following would be an INADEQUATE response to hidden upstream labour risks?

options.text: Using investigation findings to identify areas requiring remediation.
Checking whether stated commitments produce changes in practice.
Examining recruitment and working conditions beyond a direct supplier.
Assuming that the absence of abuse at a first-tier supplier establishes the absence of abuse throughout the chain.
Considering how purchasing arrangements connect a company to upstream activity.

questions.explanation: Hidden upstream conditions cannot be ruled out merely by examining one direct supplier. The article illustrates the need for visibility and action across supply-chain relationships.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 17 — Nestlé: corporate conduct and responsibility; assigned week(s): 9

questions.stem: With reference to the core article on KitKat ending its Fairtrade link, which ONE of the following statements about certification arrangements is TRUE?

options.text: All certification schemes necessarily provide the same price floor and premium.
The article concerns packaging design rather than terms affecting cocoa producers.
Using another certification means the company has stopped using any external scheme.
Fairtrade’s minimum-price and premium arrangements cannot simply be assumed to be identical to the terms of Rainforest Alliance certification.
A change in certification guarantees that every producer’s income will increase.

questions.explanation: Fairtrade’s floor-price and premium arrangements cannot be assumed to match the terms of another certification. A changed label does not itself establish a producer income gain.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 18 — KitKat ends Fairtrade link

questions.stem: The KitKat article reports Nestlé’s statement that it would maintain its cocoa spending and support farmers’ transition to another certification. Which ONE of the following conclusions would NOT follow from that statement alone?

options.text: Every individual farmer is guaranteed the same income and benefits after the change.
The company has presented a response to concerns about the transition.
Certification terms should be compared as well as aggregate spending.
A corporate commitment can be examined against subsequent implementation.
The distribution of spending among farmers remains relevant.

questions.explanation: Unchanged aggregate spending does not guarantee identical individual incomes or equivalent minimum-price and premium arrangements.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 18 — KitKat ends Fairtrade link; assigned week(s): 9

questions.stem: With reference to the KitKat article, which ONE of the following correctly distinguishes two certification changes mentioned in the report?

options.text: Rainforest Alliance was created by Nestlé solely for KitKat.
KitKat and Sainsbury’s were both adopting the same newly created in-house scheme.
KitKat’s move to Rainforest Alliance is a move to another external certification, whereas the cited Sainsbury’s tea example concerned its own scheme.
The Sainsbury’s example establishes that Rainforest Alliance is a supermarket-owned label.
Every certification change mentioned in the article occurred in the same product and year.

questions.explanation: The article distinguishes KitKat’s Rainforest Alliance transition from the earlier Sainsbury’s tea example; the schemes and contexts should not be conflated.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 18 — KitKat ends Fairtrade link; assigned week(s): 9

questions.stem: According to the Fairtrade comparison in the KitKat article, why is it insufficient to say only that a replacement scheme is also a certification?

options.text: A certification label establishes the exact income of every farmer.
Any change in label proves that no farmer receives support.
Certification arrangements concern packaging alone and cannot affect producers.
All certification schemes are required to provide identical producer payments.
The existence of a label does not establish equivalence in minimum-price protection, premiums or producer terms.

questions.explanation: The article highlights the specific minimum-price and premium features of Fairtrade. A shared category of “certification” does not demonstrate equivalent arrangements.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 18 — KitKat ends Fairtrade link; assigned week(s): 9

chapters.title: Week 10 — Big Tobacco, Oil and Pharma
chapters.description: Outline-assigned reading coverage; this is not confirmation of lecture delivery. Five options; single answer; AI-written practice.

questions.stem: According to the core article on Big Oil, plastics and Africa, which ONE of the following strategies was being reported in relation to Kenya?

options.text: A verified worldwide end to fossil-fuel companies’ involvement in plastic production.
Industry lobbying to influence trade negotiations and weaken Kenya’s restrictions on plastics and waste imports.
A completed agreement guaranteeing that all imported plastic would be recycled safely.
A campaign to exclude industry interests from international trade negotiations.
A requirement that every exporting company remove all packaging from its products.

questions.explanation: The article reports lobbying around trade negotiations and Kenyan plastics restrictions, not a verified guarantee of safe recycling or the end of plastic production.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 19 — Big Oil looks to flood Africa with plastic

questions.stem: According to the Big Oil and plastics reading, which ONE of the following best explains the industry’s interest in expanding plastics markets?

options.text: The existence of a market establishes that importing countries face no environmental costs.
Demand for plastics proves that trade rules cannot influence business strategy.
Plastics remove every link between petrochemicals and fossil-fuel businesses.
Expansion means that waste-management capacity is already adequate everywhere.
Plastics can offer a growth outlet as other parts of the fossil-fuel business face pressures.

questions.explanation: The article connects petrochemical expansion and plastics demand to the oil industry’s commercial strategy amid pressures elsewhere in its business.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 19 — Big Oil looks to flood Africa with plastic; assigned week(s): 10

questions.stem: With reference to the article on plastics and Kenya, which ONE of the following identifies the ethical issue raised by using trade negotiations to challenge domestic restrictions?

options.text: A trade negotiation is incapable of affecting environmental regulation.
Industrial lobbying can influence the balance between commercial market access and a country’s environmental protections.
The presence of negotiators proves that affected communities have equal influence.
Any domestic restriction establishes that no recycled material has economic value.
Market access necessarily has priority over public-health and waste concerns.

questions.explanation: The reported lobbying raises questions about corporate power and the effect of trade arrangements on domestic protections, not merely the existence of product demand.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 19 — Big Oil looks to flood Africa with plastic; assigned week(s): 10

questions.stem: The plastics article reports exports described as material for recycling, while also describing waste reaching rivers and oceans. Which ONE of the following is the strongest inference?

options.text: The possibility of recycling eliminates responsibility for difficult-to-process waste.
The stated purpose of recycling does not itself establish effective collection, processing and environmental outcomes.
Waste exports necessarily contain no material that could be recovered.
All exported material is proved to have been safely recycled.
Calling a shipment recyclable establishes sufficient local processing capacity.

questions.explanation: The source distinguishes a recycling rationale from actual disposal outcomes and capacity. Neither universal success nor universal impossibility follows.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 19 — Big Oil looks to flood Africa with plastic; assigned week(s): 10

questions.stem: With reference to the core reading on ILSI and food policy, which ONE of the following identifies the central concern about industry participation?

options.text: Industry funding and institutional access can create conflicts of interest in research and public-health policy.
Non-profit status prevents an organisation from having any conflict of interest.
A scientific-sounding name establishes independence from commercial influence.
Industry participation is sufficient to prove that every individual study is false.
The presence of academics removes the need to examine funding or governance.

questions.explanation: Funding and access to policy institutions can create conflicts of interest. These concerns require examination without assuming every associated study is necessarily false.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 20 — Industry influence on global food policy

questions.stem: According to the ILSI reading, why is an organisation’s non-profit status not a complete answer to questions about scientific independence?

options.text: A legal organisational form does not settle how funding, governance and institutional roles may influence an agenda.
Non-profit status establishes that every recommendation is free from competing interests.
Non-profit status proves that every study associated with the organisation is false.
Non-profit organisations cannot receive industry funding.
Only organisations that sell products can participate in policy discussions.

questions.explanation: The reading examines institutional relationships and conflicts of interest. Non-profit status neither removes those questions nor proves all findings invalid.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 20 — Industry influence on global food policy; assigned week(s): 10

questions.stem: A policy panel includes an expert with industry-linked institutional roles. With reference to the ILSI article, which ONE of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Accept the recommendation solely because the expert holds an academic title.
Reject every factual claim without examining any methods or evidence.
Examine relevant funding, roles, selection processes and the evidence supporting recommendations.
Assume that industry links cannot affect which questions receive attention.
Treat disclosure as proof that no conflict can affect the process.

questions.explanation: The article supports scrutiny of evidence and institutional influence. Expertise and disclosure matter but do not settle all questions about independence.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 20 — Industry influence on global food policy; assigned week(s): 10

questions.stem: With reference to the ILSI reading, which ONE of the following statements is FALSE?

options.text: Identifying an industry connection proves, without further inquiry, that every associated result is false.
Scientific claims should be assessed using evidence as well as relevant conflicts of interest.
Funding can affect a research agenda without requiring every published finding to be fabricated.
The composition of influential bodies can matter for public-health policy.
An organisation’s public presentation can be compared with its funding and governance.

questions.explanation: A conflict of interest creates reasons for scrutiny, not a deductive proof that all associated findings are false. This preserves the distinction between institutional influence and evidence evaluation.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 20 — Industry influence on global food policy; assigned week(s): 10

chapters.title: Week 11 — Social Media and Ultra-processed Food

questions.stem: With reference to the Pringles and Subway tax cases in the core reading, which ONE of the following conclusions would be INCORRECT?

options.text: A court’s reasoning should be read in its legal context.
A product’s marketing description does not necessarily determine its tax classification.
A favourable food classification for tax purposes establishes that the product is nutritionally healthy.
A tax decision can depend on the particular statutory definition at issue.
A legal category and a nutritional evaluation need not answer the same question.

questions.explanation: Tax categories answer a particular legal question; they do not by themselves establish a product’s healthfulness or settle all marketing claims.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 21 — Pringles and Subway VAT rulings

questions.stem: With reference to the Pringles and Subway tax cases, which ONE of the following is important when comparing the rulings?

options.text: A classification under one statute must apply identically under every other statute.
The applicable statutory wording and jurisdiction may differ, so the legal questions must be identified separately.
The products’ brand names determine the outcome without reference to ingredients or legislation.
A tax ruling is an international scientific definition binding on all nutrition research.
The existence of litigation establishes that consumers have suffered the same harm in both cases.

questions.explanation: The cases involve particular tax categories in different legal settings. Their scope cannot be treated as a universal nutritional classification.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 21 — Pringles and Subway VAT rulings; assigned week(s): 11

questions.stem: The Subway report compares sugar content expressed as a percentage of the weight of flour with a threshold in the relevant tax definition of bread. Which ONE of the following interpretations is correct?

options.text: The statutory threshold establishes the medically safe sugar intake for every customer.
The flour-based percentage is necessarily the percentage of the entire finished sandwich.
A product outside that tax definition cannot contain any flour.
The ruling establishes that every food sold by the same company has the same composition.
The comparison concerns a particular legal definition and denominator, not the sugar percentage of the whole finished meal.

questions.explanation: The source’s sugar comparison uses flour weight and a statutory bread definition. It should not be converted into a finished-meal percentage or a clinical recommendation.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 21 — Pringles and Subway VAT rulings; assigned week(s): 11

questions.stem: With reference to the Pringles part of Reading 21, which ONE of the following best explains why an argument about whether a product is “made from potato” matters?

options.text: It removes the need to identify which law and ruling are being discussed.
It settles whether every advertising claim about the product is ethical.
It addresses wording relevant to a VAT category rather than independently determining the product’s overall nutritional quality.
It establishes that VAT categories are simply rankings from healthy to unhealthy.
It proves that a product cannot contain more than one ingredient.

questions.explanation: The dispute concerns statutory classification for tax. The legal meaning and outcome must be kept distinct from wider ethical or nutritional assessments.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 21 — Pringles and Subway VAT rulings; assigned week(s): 11

questions.stem: According to the core reading explaining Cambridge Analytica, which ONE of the following best describes the process connecting data, inferred traits and targeted messaging?

options.text: Use questionnaire and like data to train predictions about traits, then use inferred profiles to support targeted messaging.
Replace statistical inference with a complete questionnaire administered to every person targeted.
Infer each individual’s vote with certainty from a single like, without a training process.
Collect no personal data and assign personality traits purely at random.
Prove that every person receiving an advertisement changed their vote because of it.

questions.explanation: The article explains statistical inference from training data and targeting based on inferred traits; it does not establish certainty about each individual vote or advert effect.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 22 — How Cambridge Analytica worked

questions.stem: According to the Cambridge Analytica reading, which ONE of the following correctly distinguishes inputs from predicted outputs in the personality-modelling process?

options.text: Patterns of likes can serve as inputs used to predict personality traits.
The presence of any like establishes the person’s future vote with certainty.
Votes must be known before likes can be observed.
Likes are the predicted personality traits and questionnaire answers are always advertisements.
An advertisement is a verified personality score for its viewer.

questions.explanation: The reading describes using questionnaire and like data to model relationships and predict traits. Likes are features, not the trait labels or certain future votes.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 22 — How Cambridge Analytica worked; assigned week(s): 11

questions.stem: With reference to the Cambridge Analytica article, why is data containing both observed likes and questionnaire-based personality information useful for training a model?

options.text: It means that no assumptions or statistical inference are involved.
It establishes that every user has completed an identical questionnaire.
It guarantees that the model causes any later political decision.
It removes every need to evaluate the model’s predictive performance.
It permits relationships between observable features and measured traits to be estimated before predicting traits for other users.

questions.explanation: Training data pair features with measured outcomes so that relationships can be learned. Prediction for others remains an inference, not certainty or causal proof.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 22 — How Cambridge Analytica worked; assigned week(s): 11

questions.stem: A campaign uses a personality model to select different messages for different audiences. According to the Cambridge Analytica reading, which ONE of the following would be an UNSUPPORTED additional claim?

options.text: Predicting a trait and persuading a person are distinct outcomes.
Targeting a message proves that the message changed the recipient’s vote.
The model can make predictions based on patterns in available data.
Evidence of predictive performance is not identical to evidence of persuasive impact.
The campaign can use inferred traits to inform message selection.

questions.explanation: The article’s account of profiling and targeting does not itself establish the causal impact of each message on voting behaviour.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Reading 22 — How Cambridge Analytica worked; assigned week(s): 11

chapters.title: Tutorial 1 — Child Labour and Ethical Sourcing

questions.stem: With reference to the low-cost clothing case-study for the first discussion group, which ONE of the following combinations most accurately identifies the buyer’s central ethical conflict?

options.text: Promotion and cost targets conflict with concerns about worker safety, education and family livelihoods.
A choice between a legally verified supplier and a supplier already convicted of every reported practice.
A choice between suppliers that differ in price but have no differences relevant to ethics.
A conflict caused solely by the buyer’s dislike of travelling overseas.
A dilemma that disappears because the retailer deals through an agent.

questions.explanation: The written case places career incentives and cost targets alongside worker safety, children’s education and household livelihoods, creating a multi-stakeholder dilemma.
questions.source: AI-written practice; MG2008 Discussion Group One — Case-study One

questions.stem: In the first discussion case, the retailer’s agent is certified as an ethical provider, but the buyer has directly observed troubling conditions further along the supply chain. Which ONE of the following conclusions about certification is justified?

options.text: Certification does not remove the need to investigate the conditions actually observed in the supply chain.
An honest agent cannot be connected with a supply chain containing harmful conditions.
Certification establishes that every subcontracted family unit has been independently inspected.
Certification transfers all ethical responsibility away from the retailer and buyer.
The buyer must disregard direct observations that conflict with the certificate.

questions.explanation: Directly observed conditions still need investigation. An agent’s certification cannot by itself establish that every subcontracted activity is acceptable.
questions.source: AI-written practice; MG2008 Discussion Group One — Case-study One

questions.stem: With reference to the first discussion case, which ONE of the following best explains why withdrawing a supplier contract immediately is not automatically a complete ethical solution?

options.text: The existence of worse alternatives makes hazardous conditions ethically acceptable without further enquiry.
Withdrawal would necessarily benefit every child by creating an immediate school place and income replacement.
It may remove income from families whose realistic alternatives must also be assessed.
Current family income makes children’s education irrelevant.
The supplier’s willingness to accept the contract establishes informed consent by all workers.

questions.explanation: Withdrawal may threaten livelihoods, so realistic alternatives matter. This is not a reason to disregard safety or education or to accept the status quo uncritically.
questions.source: AI-written practice; MG2008 Discussion Group One — Case-study One

questions.stem: With reference to the first discussion case, which ONE of the following best describes what a utilitarian analysis of the sourcing decision should compare?

options.text: Whether the agent has a certificate, without examining consequences.
The likely benefits and harms of realistic alternatives across all affected groups.
Only the supplier’s ability to meet the retailer’s target price.
Whether the buyer’s personal intention is good, regardless of outcomes.
Only the buyer’s prospects of obtaining promotion.

questions.explanation: Utilitarian case analysis compares likely consequences of feasible options for all affected groups, not only the buyer’s promotion or the retailer’s target cost.
questions.source: AI-written practice; MG2008 Discussion Group One — Case-study One; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 4, Part 2 — Utilitarianism

questions.stem: With reference to the first discussion case, which ONE of the following would be most central to a duty- and rights-based critique of the proposed sourcing arrangement?

options.text: Whether workers are being treated with dignity and whether safety and education claims are being respected.
Whether aggregate profit is high enough to make every other consideration unnecessary.
Whether the manager’s local acceptance of the practice establishes its moral validity.
Whether the buyer can avoid being blamed by referring to the agent’s certificate.
Whether the buyer’s preferred outcome benefits their own career over the longer term.

questions.explanation: Duty- and rights-based analysis examines treatment, dignity and relevant rights rather than allowing aggregate profit or certification alone to settle the issue.
questions.source: AI-written practice; MG2008 Discussion Group One — Case-study One; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 1 — Kantian Ethics; [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences

questions.stem: With reference to the first discussion case, which option gives the COMPLETE set of matters that should inform a serious ethical response below?

options.text: Hazardous machinery and other working conditions.
Children’s education and future opportunities.
Household incomes and realistic alternatives to the present work.
a) and b) above.
a), b) and c) above.

questions.explanation: Safety, education and livelihoods all appear in the case. A response that ignores any one of them leaves a material part of the dilemma unexamined.

questions.stem: With reference to the first discussion group’s micro/meso/macro framework, which ONE of the following pairings is correct?

options.text: Micro: all country-level institutions; meso: only the buyer’s feelings; macro: only the retailer’s target price.

Micro: factory management and worker conditions; meso: local community and livelihood dependencies; macro: national rules and wider context.
Micro: national legislation; meso: an individual worker’s personnel record; macro: the factory’s lighting.

questions.stem: With reference to the historical case-study “Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor”, which ONE of the following is central to the company’s business model at the time of the case?

options.text: A wholesale-only model with no direct relationship with household customers.
Interest-free grants funded entirely by charitable donations.
Credit-financed sales of household goods to customers often underserved by conventional banks.
Cash-only sales of unbranded essentials to customers with high regular salaries.
Exclusion of applicants who do not already own a conventional bank account.

questions.explanation: The case centres on providing credit-financed access to durable household goods for people often excluded from conventional banking.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor — Case pp. 10–11.

questions.stem: According to the historical Casas Bahia case, which ONE of the following statements about the assessment of customers seeking credit is TRUE?

options.text: Credit analysts were prohibited from asking about a customer’s circumstances.
Every applicant was accepted without any credit assessment.
The company relied only on a current account balance supplied by a bank.
Every customer without a prior bank loan was automatically rejected.
Credit analysts could use personal assessment where standard records or automated scoring did not settle an application.

questions.explanation: The case describes credit analysts making personal assessments when standard records or automated scoring were insufficient, rather than universal acceptance or rejection.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor — Case p. 11.

questions.stem: With reference to the historical Casas Bahia case, which ONE of the following best describes the commercial effect of requiring instalment payments to be made in the stores?

options.text: It supported ongoing relationships and created opportunities for cross-selling.
It removed the retailer’s need to maintain customer information.
It prevented customers from seeing other products while repaying.
It meant that the company could not encourage repeat purchases.
It guaranteed that credit purchases cost the same as cash purchases.

questions.explanation: In-store repayments maintained relationships and repeatedly exposed customers to products, giving the retailer opportunities to cross-sell.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor — Case pp. 12–13.

questions.stem: With reference to the historical Casas Bahia case, which ONE of the following observations most clearly explains why a low default rate cannot, by itself, establish customer wellbeing?

options.text: The company had no way to identify whether customers repaid.
The company refused to let customers visit the stores after their first purchase.
Customers were prevented from buying household goods on credit.
A customer described postponing replacement of damaged sandals in order to keep instalments up to date.
Every credit purchase was provided without interest or additional cost.

questions.explanation: The sandals example shows that timely repayment can involve foregoing other needs; low default therefore does not measure the whole welfare effect.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor — Case p. 12.

questions.stem: According to the historical Casas Bahia case, which ONE of the following comparisons between default rates on different products is TRUE?

options.text: Furniture had a lower default rate than portable items, with the ease of locating and recovering goods identified as relevant.
The case gives no connection between recovery of goods and repayment patterns.
Furniture had the highest default solely because it was installed in customers’ homes.
Portable items had no default because they were easier for the retailer to recover.
Default was identical across all product categories.

questions.explanation: The case links furniture’s lower default with being installed and more readily recovered, unlike portable items that were harder to monitor.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor — Case p. 12.

questions.stem: A customer can meet a small monthly instalment but does not compare the total credit cost with the price of buying the item for cash. With reference to the ethical issues in the Casas Bahia case, which ONE of the following concerns is most directly raised?

options.text: Accepting a payment schedule proves full understanding of every alternative.
The ability to repay one instalment establishes that no other needs are displaced.
The retailer’s commercial success establishes that the customer receives the best possible deal.
A small instalment establishes that credit is costless.
Monthly affordability may obscure the total financing cost and its effect on the household budget.

questions.explanation: A manageable monthly payment does not reveal the full financing cost or what else the household must forgo. Informed comparison requires attention to both.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor

questions.stem: With reference to the original Casas Bahia case-study, which ONE of the following correctly explains the commercial significance of the 2002 debt pardon?

options.text: It combined a tax deduction with a marketing opportunity to bring previously inactive or blacklisted customers back.
It had no financial or commercial advantage of any kind for the company.
It permanently prevented the affected customers from buying on credit again.
It forgave every future credit purchase for every customer indefinitely.
It was described as a government payment replacing the company’s lost revenue.

questions.explanation: The case describes the write-off as both tax-reducing and commercially useful in bringing customers back. It was not presented as having no business advantage.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor — Case p. 13; this tests the mechanism rather than repeating official sample 6.

questions.stem: With reference to the historical Casas Bahia case, which ONE of the following statements is FALSE?

options.text: Repayment behaviour and household wellbeing are related but different matters.
Credit assessment was central to extending access while managing risk.
The low average default rate establishes that customers never sacrificed other needs in order to repay.
In-store repayments supported continuing contact with customers.
Default rates varied between product types.

questions.explanation: The case’s customer-hardship example prevents low default from being treated as proof that there was no welfare cost.
questions.source: AI-written practice; Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor

chapters.title: Tutorial 3 — Junk Food and ILSI
chapters.description: Source-grounded tutorial practice in the five-option official sample style.

questions.stem: With reference to the final discussion group’s instruction to critique ILSI, which ONE of the following approaches best meets the purpose of the assignment?

options.text: Accept the website’s claims as sufficient because the organisation is a non-profit.
Use the presence of academic contributors as proof of complete independence.
Assess credibility by the scientific appearance of the name without investigating the organisation.
Reject every individual research finding solely because an industry participant is involved.
Compare the organisation’s self-presentation with independent evidence about funding, governance and influence.

questions.explanation: The assignment asks for a critique comparing self-presentation with other evidence. Funding, governance and influence are relevant; names and status alone are insufficient.
questions.source: AI-written practice; MG2008 Third Discussion Group Details; Reading 20 — Industry influence on global food policy

questions.stem: According to Moss, in “The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food”, the “bliss point” refers to which ONE of the following?

options.text: A legal limit requiring every product to contain no added sugar.
The lowest retail price at which all consumers can afford a product.
A sensory level that maximises liking, rather than an assumption that more sweetness is always better.
A measure proving that a product cannot be overconsumed.
The point at which consumers fully understand every long-term health effect.

questions.explanation: The bliss point is an optimum in liking; adding more sweetness beyond that point does not necessarily increase appeal.
questions.source: AI-written practice; The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food

questions.stem: According to Moss, in “The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food”, which ONE of the following statements about “sensory-specific satiety” is TRUE?

options.text: A strong, distinctive flavour can reduce the desire to continue eating, helping explain the commercial appeal of more complex formulations.
It measures whether the retail price makes a product affordable to all consumers.
Consumers become unable to distinguish flavours as soon as they have eaten one serving.
The concept establishes that every highly palatable product has no calories.
Increasing sweetness always increases liking at the same rate.

questions.explanation: Sensory-specific satiety describes reduced desire in response to a pronounced flavour. The article connects avoiding an overriding single flavour with continued consumption.
questions.source: AI-written practice; The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food

questions.stem: With reference to the Lunchables discussion in Moss’s article, which ONE of the following ideas became central to marketing the product to children?

options.text: The view that parents’ time pressures played no role in developing the product.
The promise that every tray contained only unprocessed fresh ingredients.
The claim that children were uninterested in making choices about food.
The decision to stop using taste or convenience in the product’s positioning.
The feeling of control involved in choosing and assembling what they would eat.

questions.explanation: Moss describes positioning Lunchables around children’s feeling of choice and control, not only the physical contents of the tray.
questions.source: AI-written practice; The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food; MG2008 Third Discussion Group Details

questions.stem: According to the food scientist quoted by Moss in the discussion of Cheetos, “vanishing caloric density” refers to which ONE of the following claims?

options.text: Consumers can infer a product’s full nutritional value from its texture alone.
The product’s price falls as more units are sold.
The food’s calories physically disappear when it is chewed.
Rapid melting in the mouth can make a food seem less calorific and encourage continued eating.
Every light-textured food contains less energy per gram than fresh fruit.

questions.explanation: The article reports the scientist’s claim that rapid melting can make a food seem less calorific and encourage eating. It does not mean the food’s calories disappear.
questions.source: AI-written practice; The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food — This tests the article’s reported account, not an independently verified clinical rule.

questions.stem: Moss reports that Finland’s reduction in salt consumption occurred alongside improved medical care and a large decline in deaths from stroke and heart disease. Which ONE of the following interpretations best preserves the qualification in the account?

options.text: The article establishes that a warning label alone caused every avoided death.
An observed health improvement means there is no further reason to examine industry practices.
The reported change supports examining public-health interventions, but the whole decline should not be attributed to salt reduction alone while ignoring improved medical care.
The historical example establishes identical numerical effects for every country and period.
The presence of more than one contributing factor proves that salt intake was irrelevant.

questions.explanation: The source mentions both reduced salt intake and improved care. A careful interpretation does not turn the entire historical association into a single-cause effect.
questions.source: AI-written practice; The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food
